title: Complex colour-filter reasoning
question: An ideal red filter is placed in front of a white screen. A blue filter is then placed after the red filter. The red filter transmits red light only, and the blue filter transmits blue light only. What reaches the screen?

options.text: Red light, because the first filter determines the final colour.
Blue light, because the second filter replaces the first filter's transmitted colour.
White light, because the filters together transmit all primary colours.
Ideally, no visible light, because no wavelength is transmitted by both filters.

explanation:
ing

An ideal red filter is placed in front of a white screen. A blue filter is then placed after the red filter. The red filter transmits red light only, and the blue filter transmits blue light only. What reaches the screen?

A) Red light, because the first filter determines the final colour.

B) Blue light, because the second filter replaces the first filter's transmitted colour.

C) White light, because the filters together transmit all primary colours.

D) Ideally, no visible light, because no wavelength is transmitted by both filters.

**Correct Answer: D**

**Reason:** The red filter removes the blue component before the beam reaches the second filter. The blue filter then blocks the red light that remains. Ideal filters therefore transmit no visible light in this arrangement.

title: A prism and a parallel-sided glass slab
question: Which statement correctly compares a triangular glass prism with a parallel-sided glass slab, assuming the surrounding medium is air?

options.text: Both always produce the same angular dispersion and the same emergent direction.
A prism generally produces net angular deviation and dispersion; a parallel-sided slab generally produces a lateral displacement while the emergent ray remains parallel to the incident ray.
A slab produces no refraction because its opposite faces are parallel.
A prism cannot disperse white light unless its faces are parallel.

explanation: The two faces of a parallel-sided slab have parallel normals, so the angular effects generally cancel and the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, though laterally displaced. A prism has non-parallel refracting faces, producing net deviation and, for white light, dispersion.

title: Which statement about the spectrum is false?
question: Which statement about the spectrum is false?

options.text: A monochromatic beam can be deviated by a prism without being split into a range of colours.
A continuous spectrum contains an uninterrupted range of wavelengths over the relevant interval.
A line spectrum can help identify an emitting element.
Every spectrum formed by a prism must be continuous, regardless of the nature of the source.

explanation: A prism disperses the wavelengths present in the incident light; it does not determine whether the source emits a continuous range or discrete wavelengths. A continuous source can produce a continuous spectrum, while a low-pressure emitting gas can produce a line spectrum.

title: Complex electromagnetic-wave comparison
question: Consider three electromagnetic radiations P, Q and R in vacuum. Their frequencies satisfy f_P<f_Q<f_R. Which set of conclusions is necessarily correct?

options.text: v_P<v_Q<v_R and E_P<E_Q<E_R
v_P=v_Q=v_R and lambda_P<lambda_Q<lambda_R
v_P=v_Q=v_R, lambda_P>lambda_Q>lambda_R, and E_P<E_Q<E_R
v_P>v_Q>v_R and E_P=E_Q=E_R

explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel at speed c in vacuum. Since c=flambda, increasing frequency means decreasing wavelength. Since E=hf, photon energy increases with frequency.

title: Integrated spectrum problem
question: A white-light source produces a spectrum through a prism. A green filter is placed in the separated beam so that only green light is transmitted. The transmitted light then enters a second prism. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The second prism can refract the green beam, but it cannot reconstruct the original white-light spectrum from the green component alone.
The second prism must recreate all seven colours because every prism produces dispersion.
The green filter increases the frequency of green light so that the second prism can generate the missing colours.
The second prism converts green light into white light by changing its wavelength while keeping its speed constant in glass.

explanation: The green filter removes the other spectral components. The second prism can refract the remaining green light, but it cannot restore wavelengths that are no longer present in the beam. Dispersion separates existing wavelengths; it does not create missing components.

title: Board-style — Combined prism reasoning
question: A narrow beam of white light passes through a glass prism and forms a spectrum on a screen. Which set of statements is correct? I. Violet is generally deviated more than red. II. The frequency of each colour remains unchanged while it passes through the prism. III. The wavelength of each colour is generally smaller inside glass than in air. IV. The prism increases the frequency of violet light more than that of red light.

options.text: I and II only
II, III and IV only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only

explanation:
ing

A narrow beam of white light passes through a glass prism and forms a spectrum on a screen. Which set of statements is correct?

I. Violet is generally deviated more than red.

II. The frequency of each colour remains unchanged while it passes through the prism.

III. The wavelength of each colour is generally smaller inside glass than in air.

IV. The prism increases the frequency of violet light more than that of red light.

A) I and II only

B) II, III and IV only

C) I, II and III only

D) I, III and IV only

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:** Ordinary glass has a higher refractive index for violet than for red, so violet is deviated more. Frequency remains unchanged at stationary boundaries, while the reduced speed in glass reduces wavelength. A prism does not increase a light wave's frequency.

title: Board-style — Minimum deviation and prism geometry
question: A ray passes through a prism of angle A. At the position of minimum deviation, the angle of deviation is delta_m. Which relation is correct?

options.text: i=e, r₁=r₂=A/2, and delta_m=2i-A
i≠ e, r₁+r₂=2A, and delta_m=i+e+A
i=e, r₁=r₂=A, and delta_m=i+e
i=e=0, and delta_m=0 for every prism

explanation: At minimum deviation, the ray path through the prism is symmetric. Thus i=e, and since r₁+r₂=A, each internal refraction angle equals A/2. Using delta=i+e-A, we obtain delta_m=2i-A.

title: Board-style — Dispersion versus recombination
question: A student uses two identical glass prisms, with the second inverted relative to the first. White light enters the first prism. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The first prism converts white light into seven new frequencies, which the second prism destroys.
The second prism can recombine the colours only if it changes every colour's frequency.
The two prisms must always produce a completely dark screen because their deviations cancel.
With suitable alignment, the second prism can reverse the dispersion and bring the separated colours together approximately as white light.

explanation: The first prism separates the component wavelengths. An inverted second prism can undo the angular separation when suitably aligned. The frequencies of the individual components remain unchanged; their directions are altered.

title: Board-style — Refraction at a boundary
question: Monochromatic light of frequency f travels from air into glass of refractive index n. Which set of changes is correct, taking the refractive index of air as approximately 1?

options.text: Speed becomes nc, wavelength becomes nlambda, and frequency stays f.
Speed becomes c/n, wavelength becomes lambda/n, and frequency stays f.
Speed becomes c/n, wavelength stays lambda, and frequency becomes f/n.
Speed stays c, wavelength becomes lambda/n, and frequency becomes nf.

explanation: In glass, v=c/n. Frequency remains f, so lambda'=v/f=(c/n)/f=lambda/n. Both speed and wavelength decrease, but frequency remains unchanged.

title: Board-style — Identifying a pure spectrum
question: Which experimental arrangement is most likely to produce a pure spectrum of white light?

options.text: A broad slit, a prism and a screen placed very close to the prism
A white screen viewed through a coloured glass plate without a slit
A narrow slit, a collimating arrangement, a prism and a suitably positioned screen
A broad source placed directly against a screen, without a dispersing element

explanation: A narrow slit helps reduce overlap of the images of different wavelengths. A collimating arrangement and a suitable prism–screen geometry improve spectral separation. A prism alone does not guarantee a pure spectrum if the source slit is too broad or the arrangement is unsuitable.

title: Board-style — Colour of an object under selective illumination
question: A red flower and a white sheet are illuminated by pure blue light. Assume the flower reflects red strongly but absorbs most blue light. Which observation is most likely?

options.text: Both appear bright red.
The flower appears black or very dark, while the white sheet appears blue.
The flower appears white, while the sheet appears black.
Both appear white because blue light contains all visible colours.

explanation: The flower cannot reflect red light that is not present in the illumination, and it absorbs most of the incident blue light. It therefore appears dark. The white sheet reflects the incident blue light and appears blue.

title: Board-style — Filter combinations
question: White light passes successively through an ideal magenta filter and an ideal yellow filter. Magenta transmits red and blue; yellow transmits red and green. Which component emerges?

options.text: Red only
Green only
Blue only
White light

explanation: Magenta transmits red and blue, whereas yellow transmits red and green. Red is the only component transmitted by both filters. The second filter cannot restore the green component removed by the first filter or the blue component it absorbs.

title: Board-style — Atmospheric scattering
question: Consider the following statements about the colour of the sky and the Sun at sunset. I. Small atmospheric molecules scatter shorter visible wavelengths more strongly under Rayleigh conditions. II. The direct sunlight reaching an observer at sunset is often relatively richer in red and orange wavelengths. III. The blue appearance of the sky is caused mainly by the Sun emitting more blue photons than photons of every other visible colour under all conditions. IV. Rayleigh scattering varies approximately as 1/lambda⁴. Which option is correct?

options.text: I and III only
II and III only
I, II and IV only
I, II, III and IV

explanation: Statements I, II and IV describe Rayleigh scattering and the longer atmospheric path at sunset. Statement III is incorrect because the sky's colour depends on atmospheric scattering, solar spectrum, transmission and visual response—not simply on the Sun emitting more blue light under all conditions.

title: Board-style — Electromagnetic spectrum ordering
question: Four radiations are labelled P, Q, R and S. Their wavelengths satisfy lambda_P>lambda_Q>lambda_R>lambda_S. Which statement must be true in vacuum?

options.text: Their frequencies satisfy f_P>f_Q>f_R>f_S.
Their speeds satisfy v_P>v_Q>v_R>v_S.
Their photon energies satisfy E_P>E_Q>E_R>E_S.
Their frequencies and photon energies satisfy f_P<f_Q<f_R<f_S and E_P<E_Q<E_R<E_S.

explanation: In vacuum, c=flambda, so frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength. Photon energy is E=hf, so photon energy also increases as wavelength decreases. All four radiations travel at the same speed in vacuum.

title: Board-style — Radiation and applications
question: Which combination is entirely correct?

options.text: Infrared — detecting bone fractures; X-rays — remote controls; ultraviolet — ordinary radio broadcasting
Microwaves — radar; infrared — thermal imaging; X-rays — medical imaging
Radio waves — fluorescence; ultraviolet — satellite navigation exclusively; gamma rays — ordinary television remote controls
Visible light — sterilising all medical instruments regardless of exposure; infrared — ionising radiation; microwaves — nuclear decay detection exclusively

explanation: Microwaves are used in radar, infrared radiation is useful for thermal imaging, and X-rays are used in medical imaging. The other combinations mismatch the radiation with its established application or make unjustified absolute claims.

title: Board-style — Assertion–Reason: ultraviolet radiation
question: Assertion (A):** Ultraviolet radiation can cause fluorescence in certain substances. **Reason (R):** Some substances absorb ultraviolet photons and subsequently emit lower-energy photons, often in the visible region.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
ultraviolet radiation

**Assertion (A):** Ultraviolet radiation can cause fluorescence in certain substances.

**Reason (R):** Some substances absorb ultraviolet photons and subsequently emit lower-energy photons, often in the visible region.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Fluorescent materials can absorb higher-energy ultraviolet photons and emit lower-energy visible photons. The emitted light is typically lower in energy because some absorbed energy is lost through non-radiative processes before emission.

title: Board-style — Comparing radiation hazards
question: Which statement is scientifically correct?

options.text: Infrared radiation is more ionising than gamma radiation because infrared is associated with heat.
All electromagnetic radiation causes ionisation whenever its intensity is sufficiently high.
X-rays and gamma rays can be ionising, whereas ordinary infrared radiation is primarily associated with vibrational excitation and heating rather than direct ionisation.
Radio waves are more ionising than ultraviolet radiation because radio waves have longer wavelengths.

explanation: Ionising ability depends strongly on photon energy, which increases with frequency. X-rays and gamma rays have sufficiently high photon energies to ionise atoms. Infrared photons have much lower energies and ordinarily produce heating rather than direct ionisation.

title: Board-style — Prism deviation and wavelength
question: A beam containing red, green and violet light enters an ordinary glass prism. Which statement is correct under normal dispersion?

options.text: Red has the highest refractive index and greatest deviation.
Violet has the highest refractive index and generally the greatest deviation; red has the lowest refractive index and generally the least deviation.
All colours have identical refractive indices because they enter the same glass.
Violet has the lowest frequency and therefore the smallest deviation.

explanation: Under normal dispersion, the refractive index of ordinary glass increases as wavelength decreases. Violet therefore has a higher refractive index and generally suffers greater deviation than red.

title: Board-style — The primary rainbow
question: Which sequence correctly describes the principal optical processes producing a primary rainbow?

options.text: Reflection from the outer surface only, followed by absorption and emission
Diffraction at entry, two internal reflections, and no refraction at exit
Refraction without dispersion, followed by total absorption inside the drop
Refraction and dispersion on entering a raindrop, one internal reflection, and refraction on emerging

explanation: In a primary rainbow, sunlight is refracted and dispersed when it enters a raindrop, undergoes one internal reflection, and is refracted again on emerging. Different wavelengths emerge in different directions.

title: Board-style — Continuous and line spectra
question: A low-pressure gas emits a spectrum consisting of several distinct bright lines against a dark background. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: The gas emits only selected wavelengths associated with transitions between discrete atomic energy levels.
The gas emits every visible wavelength continuously, but the prism removes all wavelengths between the lines.
The spectrum must be continuous because every atom contains electrons.
The gas is necessarily at a temperature of absolute zero.

explanation: Excited atoms emit photons at particular energies corresponding to allowed transitions between energy levels. These photons produce characteristic spectral lines rather than an uninterrupted continuum. The line positions can help identify the emitting substance.

title: Board-style — Why the prism does not change frequency
question: A student claims that violet light must increase its frequency when entering glass because its speed decreases and its wavelength becomes shorter. Which response is correct?

options.text: The claim is correct because frequency is directly proportional to refractive index.
The claim is correct only if the incident light is white.
The claim is incorrect because the source frequency remains unchanged at a stationary boundary; the reduced speed is accompanied by a proportionate reduction in wavelength.
The claim is incorrect because wavelength and speed remain constant in every transparent medium.

explanation: The relation v=flambda applies in the medium. Since f remains unchanged and v decreases in glass, lambda must decrease. Frequency does not rise merely because the wavelength changes.

title: Board-style — Complementary colours
question: A white screen is illuminated by red light and cyan light in suitable proportions. What is the expected result under ideal additive colour mixing?

options.text: Black, because cyan absorbs red light.
Approximately white, because cyan supplies green and blue components that complement red.
Yellow, because red and cyan always produce yellow.
Pure blue, because cyan contains no green component.

explanation: Cyan light contains green and blue components. When suitably balanced with red light, the three additive primaries are present together, producing approximately white light. The result depends on relative intensities and the illumination conditions.

title: Board-style — Electromagnetic waves and vacuum
question: Consider these statements: I. Visible light can propagate through vacuum. II. Radio waves require air to propagate. III. Electromagnetic waves in vacuum all travel at the same speed. IV. Sound can propagate through a vacuum in the same way as light. Which option is correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, II and III only
I and III only

explanation: Statements I and III are true. Radio waves are electromagnetic waves and do not require air. Sound is a mechanical wave and requires a material medium, so it cannot propagate through a perfect vacuum.

title: Board-style — Comparing photon energies
question: A photon of ultraviolet radiation has a frequency three times that of a photon of visible light. What is the ratio of their photon energies?
explanation: Photon energy is E=hf. The energy ratio is therefore equal to the frequency ratio, 3:1. The wavelength ratio would be inverse, but wavelength is not the quantity being compared.

title: Board-style — Spectrum and source characteristics
question: Which statement about a thermal source and its spectrum is most accurate?

options.text: Every hot source emits only one wavelength, regardless of temperature.
A thermal source emits a continuous range of wavelengths, and the distribution of emitted radiation depends on its temperature.
The spectrum of a thermal source is always a set of isolated lines identical to that of a low-pressure gas.
Increasing the temperature can change the amplitude of radiation but can never change its spectral distribution.

explanation: An ideal thermal source produces a continuous spectrum whose distribution depends on temperature. As temperature increases, the characteristic distribution shifts towards shorter wavelengths and the emitted power generally rises.

title: Board-style — Multi-statement analysis of a prism
question: Consider a narrow beam of white light passing through a glass prism. I. The emergent beam may be separated into different colours. II. The frequency of each component changes at the first refracting surface. III. The refractive index of ordinary glass generally differs for different visible wavelengths. IV. If monochromatic light is used instead, the prism can still deviate the beam. Which option is correct?

options.text: I, II and III only
II and IV only
I and III only
I, III and IV only

explanation: Statements I, III and IV are true. Dispersion occurs because refractive index depends on wavelength, and a prism can refract monochromatic light without forming a spectrum. Statement II is false because frequency remains unchanged across a stationary boundary.

title: Board-style — Distinguishing scattering from dispersion
question: A beam of white light passes through a clear glass prism and produces a spectrum. A separate beam passes through a colloidal suspension, making its path visible from the side. Which identification is correct?

options.text: Both observations are caused exclusively by total internal reflection.
The prism demonstrates dispersion, while the visible beam in the suspension demonstrates scattering.
The prism demonstrates fluorescence, while the suspension demonstrates only refraction.
Both observations require the light's frequency to increase.

explanation: The prism separates wavelengths because their refractive indices differ. The colloidal suspension makes the beam visible through scattering by suspended particles. These are different optical processes and neither requires an increase in light frequency.

title: Board-style — Infrared and ultraviolet detection
question: A student wants to detect infrared radiation beyond the red end of a spectrum and ultraviolet radiation beyond the violet end. Which pair of methods is appropriate?

options.text: Infrared — observe it directly with the unaided eye; ultraviolet — measure it with an ordinary sound microphone.
Infrared — use a glass prism as a detector; ultraviolet — use a radio antenna as a detector.
Infrared — use a suitable thermopile or infrared detector; ultraviolet — use a suitable fluorescent material or UV detector.
Infrared — use only a mercury thermometer regardless of intensity; ultraviolet — use an ordinary visible-light detector that is insensitive to UV.

explanation: Infrared radiation can be detected through its thermal effect or with a dedicated infrared detector. Ultraviolet can be detected using appropriate UV-sensitive instruments or by fluorescence in suitable materials. A detector must respond to the radiation being measured.

title: Board-style — Assertion–Reason: red and violet in glass
question: Assertion (A):** In ordinary glass under normal dispersion, violet light travels more slowly than red light. **Reason (R):** The refractive index of ordinary glass for violet light is generally greater than that for red light, and v=c/n.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
red and violet in glass

**Assertion (A):** In ordinary glass under normal dispersion, violet light travels more slowly than red light.

**Reason (R):** The refractive index of ordinary glass for violet light is generally greater than that for red light, and v=c/n.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Normal dispersion gives n_V>n_R. Since speed in the medium is v=c/n, violet light has the lower speed. The reason directly establishes the assertion.

title: Board-style — The limitations of colour labels
question: A spectrum is described using the conventional labels red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Each label corresponds to exactly one wavelength.
White light contains exactly seven wavelengths and no others.
The seven labels are a useful conventional division of the visible spectrum, which actually spans a continuous range of wavelengths for a continuous source.
Every spectral colour is a mixture of all the other colours in equal proportions.

explanation: The seven named colours are conventional regions of the visible spectrum, not seven isolated wavelengths. A continuous source can contain a broad range of wavelengths between and beyond these named divisions.

title: Board-style — Which statement about the spectrum is false?
question: Board-style — Which statement about the spectrum is false?

options.text: A monochromatic beam can be deviated by a prism without being split into a range of colours.
A continuous spectrum contains an uninterrupted range of wavelengths over the relevant interval.
A line spectrum can help identify an emitting element.
Every spectrum formed by a prism must be continuous, regardless of the nature of the source.

explanation: A prism disperses the wavelengths present in the incident light; it does not determine whether the source emits a continuous range or discrete wavelengths. A continuous source can produce a continuous spectrum, while a low-pressure emitting gas can produce a line spectrum.

title: Matching the radiation to its detector
question: Which set of detector–radiation matches is entirely correct?

options.text: Infrared — blackened thermopile; ultraviolet — fluorescent material; X-rays — suitable photographic film or an X-ray detector.
Infrared — ordinary radio antenna only; ultraviolet — sound microphone; X-rays — human eye alone.
Infrared — fluorescent screen only; ultraviolet — thermopile only; X-rays — ordinary glass prism alone.
Infrared — human eye alone; ultraviolet — radio receiver; X-rays — ordinary thermometer only.

explanation: Infrared can be detected through its heating effect using a suitable thermopile. Ultraviolet can produce fluorescence in appropriate materials. X-rays can be detected using suitable photographic media or electronic detectors. No single detector is universally appropriate for every radiation.

title: Assertion–Reason: the rainbow
question: Assertion (A):** A primary rainbow is formed by refraction, dispersion and one internal reflection inside raindrops. **Reason (R):** Violet light is deviated less than red light in the formation of a primary rainbow.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
the rainbow

**Assertion (A):** A primary rainbow is formed by refraction, dispersion and one internal reflection inside raindrops.

**Reason (R):** Violet light is deviated less than red light in the formation of a primary rainbow.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:** The assertion is true: the primary rainbow involves refraction and dispersion at entry, one internal reflection, and refraction at exit. The reason is false. Violet is deviated more than red in the primary rainbow, so violet appears on the inner edge and red on the outer edge.

title: Electromagnetic radiation and material media
question: Which statement is incorrect?

options.text: Electromagnetic waves can propagate through vacuum.
All electromagnetic waves travel at approximately 3×10^8 m/s in vacuum.
Sound and electromagnetic waves are both mechanical waves and require a material medium.
Infrared radiation can transfer energy to an absorbing body and produce heating.

explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and requires a material medium. Electromagnetic waves are not mechanical waves and can propagate through vacuum. The other statements correctly describe electromagnetic radiation.

title: Continuous spectrum and source identification
question: A student observes an unbroken band of colours from a source after dispersion. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The source must be a low-pressure gas emitting only a few discrete wavelengths.
The observed band is continuous over the displayed range, but the spectral appearance alone does not uniquely identify the source material.
The source must emit only seven discrete wavelengths, one for each named colour.
The source must be a monochromatic laser because the spectrum has no dark gaps.

explanation: A continuous spectrum contains an unbroken range of wavelengths across the observed band. The appearance alone does not uniquely establish the source's composition or physical state. Many thermal sources can produce continuous spectra.

title: Integrated reasoning: a prism, a filter and a detector
question: White light passes through a glass prism, then through an ideal green filter, and finally enters a second glass prism. Which statement best describes the light reaching the final detector?

options.text: The final prism must reconstruct the original full VIBGYOR spectrum because the first prism dispersed white light.
The green filter changes the frequency of every transmitted photon, allowing the second prism to recreate white light.
The final detector must receive violet light because violet is the most-deviated colour in glass.
The beam is predominantly green; the second prism can refract it, but cannot restore wavelengths removed by the filter.

explanation:
ing: a prism, a filter and a detector

White light passes through a glass prism, then through an ideal green filter, and finally enters a second glass prism. Which statement best describes the light reaching the final detector?

A) The final prism must reconstruct the original full VIBGYOR spectrum because the first prism dispersed white light.

B) The green filter changes the frequency of every transmitted photon, allowing the second prism to recreate white light.

C) The final detector must receive violet light because violet is the most-deviated colour in glass.

D) The beam is predominantly green; the second prism can refract it, but cannot restore wavelengths removed by the filter.

**Correct Answer: D**

**Reason:** The first prism separates the wavelengths in white light. The green filter transmits predominantly green light and removes most other visible components. The second prism can refract the transmitted green beam, but it cannot recreate the removed red, blue or other wavelengths. A prism separates existing wavelengths; it does not manufacture missing colours.

title: Dispersion versus refraction
question: A student argues: “A glass prism disperses white light because every colour is refracted. Therefore, a prism will produce a spectrum from any single-colour beam.” Which assessment is correct?

options.text: Correct, because refraction always separates light into seven colours.
Incorrect, because a prism can refract monochromatic light, but dispersion requires different wavelengths to undergo different deviations.
Correct, because a monochromatic beam contains equal amounts of all seven visible colours.
Incorrect, because a prism cannot refract light unless the incident beam is white.

explanation: Refraction changes the direction of light when its speed changes at a boundary. Dispersion is the separation of different wavelengths because the refractive index depends on wavelength. Monochromatic light can be refracted without producing a spectrum.

title: Assertion–Reason: frequency at a boundary
question: Assertion (A):** When violet light enters ordinary glass from air, its frequency remains unchanged. **Reason (R):** The frequency of light is determined by the source and remains continuous across a stationary boundary, while its speed and wavelength can change.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
frequency at a boundary

**Assertion (A):** When violet light enters ordinary glass from air, its frequency remains unchanged.

**Reason (R):** The frequency of light is determined by the source and remains continuous across a stationary boundary, while its speed and wavelength can change.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Frequency is fixed by the source. On entering glass, violet light travels more slowly and its wavelength decreases, but its frequency remains unchanged. The reason directly explains the assertion.

title: The order of colours in a glass prism
question: A prism produces a spectrum on a screen. A student labels the most-deviated end red and the least-deviated end violet. Which statement identifies the error?

options.text: Red is more deviated because its wavelength is longer.
Violet is least deviated because it has the highest frequency.
The labels are correct because deviation depends only on the prism angle.
The order is reversed: violet is generally most deviated and red least deviated in ordinary glass.

explanation: Ordinary glass has a higher refractive index for violet than for red. Violet therefore experiences greater net deviation. The spectrum runs VIBGYOR from the most-deviated end to the least-deviated end.

title: Minimum deviation: identifying the false statement
question: Which statement about a prism at minimum deviation is incorrect?

options.text: The angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence.
The two internal refraction angles are equal.
The angle of deviation must be zero because the path is symmetric.
Each internal refraction angle equals half the prism angle.

explanation: Symmetry gives i=e and r₁=r₂=A/2, but it does not eliminate the net deviation. A glass prism in air generally produces a non-zero minimum deviation.

title: Pure spectrum versus continuous spectrum
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a pure spectrum from a continuous spectrum?

options.text: A pure spectrum contains no overlap between neighbouring spectral images; a continuous spectrum contains an unbroken range of wavelengths.
A pure spectrum must contain dark gaps, while a continuous spectrum must contain only bright lines.
A pure spectrum is necessarily monochromatic, whereas a continuous spectrum contains only seven wavelengths.
A continuous spectrum can be produced only by a prism, while a pure spectrum can be produced only by a diffraction grating.

explanation: Purity concerns whether the images of different wavelengths overlap appreciably. Continuity concerns whether wavelengths form an uninterrupted range. These are distinct properties: a continuous spectrum can be pure if adequately resolved.

title: Assertion–Reason: recombination of colours
question: Assertion (A):** A suitably arranged inverted prism can recombine the spectrum produced by a first prism into approximately white light. **Reason (R):** The second prism produces wavelength-dependent deviations in the opposite sense, allowing the separated colours to overlap.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
recombination of colours

**Assertion (A):** A suitably arranged inverted prism can recombine the spectrum produced by a first prism into approximately white light.

**Reason (R):** The second prism produces wavelength-dependent deviations in the opposite sense, allowing the separated colours to overlap.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** The first prism disperses the white beam; the inverted second prism reverses the sense of dispersion. With suitable alignment, the colours overlap again. The second prism does not create new frequencies or convert every colour into red.

title: Newton’s disc and additive colour mixing
question: A rapidly rotating Newton’s disc appears nearly white or grey. Which inference is most scientifically justified?

options.text: Each coloured sector becomes a white pigment due to friction.
The eye integrates the rapidly changing colour stimuli, producing an approximately combined colour.
White light is a single visible wavelength that appears different when the disc stops.
The disc demonstrates that all coloured pigments reflect identical wavelengths.

explanation: Rapid rotation makes the different coloured sectors appear together because of temporal integration in vision. The resulting appearance depends on the disc's pigments, illumination and balance of colours. It does not prove that white light is monochromatic.

title: Colour of an object under coloured illumination
question: A white card, a red card and a blue card are illuminated only by ideal monochromatic green light. Which statement is correct?

options.text: All three appear equally green because the incident light is green.
The red card appears bright red because red is its permanent colour.
The white card reflects green strongly, while the red and blue cards may appear dark if they reflect little green.
All three appear black because green light cannot be reflected by opaque objects.

explanation: A white card reflects a broad range of visible wavelengths, including green. A red or blue card typically reflects its characteristic wavelengths more strongly and may absorb much of the green illumination. Thus the coloured cards can appear dark, depending on their reflectance spectra.

title: Transparent filters: selecting wavelengths
question: A cyan filter transmits green and blue light while absorbing most red light. A yellow filter transmits red and green light while absorbing most blue light. If white light passes through the cyan filter first and the yellow filter second, what is transmitted ideally?

options.text: Green light.
White light.
Cyan light.
No light at all.

explanation: The first filter transmits green and blue. The second transmits red and green. Only green is common to both transmitted sets. The second filter cannot restore wavelengths removed by the first.

title: Additive mixing versus pigment mixing
question: Which statement about additive primary colours is correct?

options.text: Red plus green light produces cyan, and blue plus red produces yellow.
Red, green and blue pigments must always produce white when mixed.
Cyan, magenta and yellow are the primary colours of additive light mixing.
Red plus green light produces yellow; green plus blue produces cyan; and blue plus red produces magenta.

explanation: Additive mixing combines emitted light. Its primary colours are red, green and blue. The pairwise combinations produce yellow, cyan and magenta respectively. Pigment mixing is subtractive and follows a different mechanism.

title: Complementary colours
question: Which pair is complementary in ideal additive colour mixing?

options.text: Red and yellow.
Green and magenta.
Blue and cyan.
Violet and red.

explanation: Magenta contains red and blue light. Adding green supplies the missing primary component, so suitably balanced green and magenta can produce white. Complementary colours combine to give white under appropriate additive conditions.

title: Rayleigh scattering and the blue sky
question: Assertion (A):** The daytime sky away from the Sun appears blue because atmospheric molecules scatter shorter visible wavelengths more strongly. **Reason (R):** Under Rayleigh conditions, scattering intensity is approximately inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
(R):** Under Rayleigh conditions, scattering intensity is approximately inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Rayleigh scattering varies approximately as 1/lambda⁴. Shorter wavelengths such as blue are scattered more strongly than longer wavelengths such as red, contributing to the blue appearance of the sky. The exact colour also depends on atmospheric conditions and human vision.

title: Red sunsets: scattering or dispersion?
question: Which explanation best accounts for the reddish appearance of the Sun near the horizon?

options.text: The atmosphere disperses sunlight exactly like a glass prism, forming a full spectrum at the observer's eye.
Red light is refracted most strongly because it has the longest wavelength.
A longer atmospheric path preferentially scatters shorter visible wavelengths out of the direct beam, leaving relatively more red and orange light.
The Sun emits only red wavelengths at sunset.

explanation:
best accounts for the reddish appearance of the Sun near the horizon?

A) The atmosphere disperses sunlight exactly like a glass prism, forming a full spectrum at the observer's eye.

B) Red light is refracted most strongly because it has the longest wavelength.

C) A longer atmospheric path preferentially scatters shorter visible wavelengths out of the direct beam, leaving relatively more red and orange light.

D) The Sun emits only red wavelengths at sunset.

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:** Near sunset, sunlight travels through a longer atmospheric path. Shorter wavelengths are scattered more strongly, so the direct beam becomes relatively richer in red and orange. Atmospheric refraction also occurs, but it is not the main explanation for the reddish colour.

title: Tyndall effect
question: Which observation most directly demonstrates the Tyndall effect?

options.text: A ray changes direction on entering a clean glass block.
A narrow beam becomes visible from the side while passing through a colloidal suspension.
A plane mirror forms a virtual image.
White light separates into a spectrum after passing through a prism.

explanation: Colloidal particles scatter light in different directions, making the path of a beam visible from the side. Refraction at a boundary and dispersion in a prism are different optical effects.

title: Danger signals and atmospheric scattering
question: Why is red commonly used for warning lights intended to be seen from a distance?

options.text: Red has the shortest wavelength and therefore the greatest Rayleigh scattering.
Red is immune to atmospheric absorption and scattering.
Red travels faster than blue in air by a large amount.
Red is generally scattered less than shorter visible wavelengths by small atmospheric molecules, helping the direct signal remain prominent.

explanation: Rayleigh scattering is weaker at longer wavelengths. Red light can therefore retain a stronger direct component through an atmosphere dominated by small scattering particles. It is not immune to attenuation, and real fog or haze may involve more complex scattering.

title: Electromagnetic spectrum: ordering by frequency
question: Which sequence correctly arranges the following electromagnetic radiations in increasing order of frequency?

options.text: Gamma rays → X-rays → ultraviolet → visible → infrared → microwaves → radio waves
Radio waves → microwaves → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-rays → gamma rays
Radio waves → infrared → microwaves → visible → X-rays → ultraviolet → gamma rays
Infrared → radio waves → microwaves → visible → ultraviolet → gamma rays → X-rays

explanation: Frequency increases in the order radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma ray. The corresponding wavelength order is reversed. Option A gives the decreasing-frequency order instead.

title: Electromagnetic waves in vacuum
question: Assertion (A):** Radio waves and visible light travel at the same speed in vacuum. **Reason (R):** All electromagnetic waves propagate in vacuum at c≈3×10^8 m/s, irrespective of their frequency.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
(R):** All electromagnetic waves propagate in vacuum at c≈3×10^8 m/s, irrespective of their frequency.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** All electromagnetic waves have the same speed in vacuum. Radio waves and visible light differ in wavelength and frequency, not in their vacuum propagation speed. In material media, propagation speeds can depend on frequency.

title: Identifying the radiation by its use
question: Which set of radiation–application matches is entirely correct?

options.text: X-rays — broadcasting radio programmes; microwaves — detecting bone fractures; ultraviolet — night-vision thermal imaging.
Gamma rays — ordinary radio reception; infrared — medical X-ray imaging; radio waves — sterilising surgical instruments.
Microwaves — radar and satellite communication; X-rays — medical imaging; ultraviolet — fluorescence and sterilisation in suitable applications.
Visible light — nuclear gamma-ray treatment; radio waves — detecting thermal emission; infrared — producing X-ray images.

explanation: Microwaves are used in radar and satellite communication; X-rays are used in medical imaging; and ultraviolet radiation can induce fluorescence and be used for sterilisation under appropriate conditions. The other options confuse applications of different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.

title: Harmful effects of electromagnetic radiation
question: Which statement is correct?

options.text: All electromagnetic radiations are equally ionising because they travel at the same speed.
Infrared radiation is always more ionising than ultraviolet radiation because it causes heating.
Radio waves always break chemical bonds more readily than gamma rays.
X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can damage tissue; ultraviolet can damage skin and eyes, while intense infrared can cause thermal injury.

explanation: Photon energy increases with frequency. X-rays and gamma rays can ionise atoms and damage biological tissue. Ultraviolet can cause skin and eye damage, while intense infrared exposure can cause heating and burns. Equal speed in vacuum does not imply equal photon energy or equal biological effects.

title: Why the sky is not normally violet
question: If violet light is scattered more strongly than blue light under Rayleigh conditions, why does the daytime sky generally appear blue rather than violet?

options.text: Violet light is never present in sunlight.
The observed colour depends on the solar spectrum, atmospheric transmission and the human eye's wavelength sensitivity, not solely on the scattering law.
Violet light travels faster than blue light in the atmosphere and therefore escapes.
Atmospheric molecules scatter violet less strongly than red.

explanation: The 1/lambda⁴ law describes how scattering varies with wavelength under the Rayleigh approximation. The perceived sky colour also depends on the spectrum reaching the atmosphere, absorption and transmission, and how the human visual system responds to different wavelengths. Scattering strength alone does not determine perceived colour.

title: The electromagnetic spectrum and photon energy
question: Which statement is correct about photons of different electromagnetic radiations?

options.text: A radio photon always has more energy than a gamma-ray photon because radio waves can carry signals over greater distances.
Photon energy depends only on the amplitude of the electromagnetic wave, not its frequency.
A gamma-ray photon has greater energy than a radio-wave photon when its frequency is higher, because E=hf.
All electromagnetic photons have equal energy because all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in vacuum.

explanation: Photon energy is E=hf. Gamma rays have much higher frequencies than radio waves and therefore much greater energy per photon. The total energy in a beam also depends on the number of photons, so photon energy and total beam energy must not be confused.

title: Refraction at the air–glass boundary
question: Which statement correctly describes light entering ordinary glass obliquely from air?

options.text: Its speed decreases, its frequency remains unchanged, and its wavelength decreases.
Its speed increases, its frequency remains unchanged, and its wavelength increases.
Its speed decreases and its frequency necessarily decreases in the same ratio.
Its speed remains unchanged, but its frequency increases to conserve energy.

explanation: The refractive index of glass is greater than that of air, so light travels more slowly in glass. Frequency remains fixed at the boundary, and lambda=v/f; hence the wavelength decreases. The change in speed does not imply a change in frequency.

title: Ordinary dispersion in glass
question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between refractive index and colour in ordinary glass under normal dispersion?

options.text: Red has the highest refractive index because its wavelength is longest.
Refractive index is independent of wavelength, so all colours travel equally fast in glass.
Violet has a lower refractive index than red because it is deviated more.
Violet generally has a higher refractive index than red, so it travels more slowly in glass and is deviated more strongly by a prism.

explanation: In ordinary glass under normal dispersion, n_V>n_R. Since v=c/n, violet travels more slowly than red in the glass. Its larger refractive index produces greater prism deviation.

title: Why a prism deviates light towards its base
question: A triangular glass prism is placed in air. Which statement best explains the general direction of the emergent ray?

options.text: The prism always bends the ray towards its apex because the apex is thinner.
The net deviation is generally towards the base because the two refractions at the non-parallel faces produce a net angular change in that direction.
The ray bends towards the base only when it is monochromatic; white light always travels straight.
The emergent ray must be parallel to the incident ray because the two refracting faces cancel one another.

explanation: At the first face, light entering glass bends towards the normal; at the second face, light leaving glass bends away from the normal. Because the faces are not parallel, the changes do not generally cancel. The net deviation is towards the prism's base.

title: Recombination and conservation of frequency
question: Which statement best explains why recombining the colours of a spectrum can restore white light without requiring a change in the frequency of each colour?

options.text: Each colour's frequency increases until all colours become identical.
The second prism converts every colour into the same wavelength.
The separated colours are redirected to overlap, and their combined visible-light stimulus can be perceived as white.
The first prism absorbs the original frequencies, and the second prism creates new frequencies.

explanation: Recombination is an optical redirection of the separated wavelengths. The second prism can bring them into overlap, restoring a combined spectrum that appears white. The individual frequencies do not need to change.

title: Refractive index from the symmetric prism position
question: A glass prism has an angle of 50^°. At minimum deviation, the angle of incidence is 40^°. What is the refractive index of the prism relative to air?

options.text: dfrac{sin25^°}{sin40^°}
dfrac{sin40^°}{sin25^°}
dfrac{sin50^°}{sin40^°}
dfrac{sin65^°}{sin25^°}

explanation:
At minimum deviation, i=e, and the internal refraction angles are equal:


r=frac A2=(50^° / 2)=25^°.


Using Snell's law at the first face,


n=(sin i / sin r)
=(sin40^° / sin25^°)
≈1.52.


Option A reverses the ratio and would incorrectly give a refractive index below one.

title: Finding the emergence angle from deviation
question: A ray passes through a prism of angle 60^°. Its angle of incidence is 47^°, and the total deviation is 32^°. Calculate its angle of emergence.
explanation:
The prism relation is


delta=i+e-A.


Rearranging,


e=delta+A-i
=32^°+60^°-47^°
=45^°.


The tempting 77^° results from adding all three angles rather than subtracting the incidence angle.

title: Refractive index and speed difference between two colours
question: In a glass sample, the refractive indices for red and violet light are 1.48 and 1.52, respectively. Calculate the difference between their speeds in the glass.
explanation:
v_R=(3×10^8 / 1.48)
≈2.0270×10^8 m/s



v_V=(3×10^8 / 1.52)
≈1.9737×10^8 m/s.


Therefore,


v_R-v_V≈5.35×10^6 m/s.


Violet travels more slowly because its refractive index is higher.

title: Finding the wavelength in a medium from frequency and refractive index
question: A monochromatic radiation has a frequency of 5×10^ Hz and enters a transparent material of refractive index 1.25. What is its wavelength inside the material?

options.text: 750 nm
600 nm
480 nm
375 nm

explanation:
The speed in the material is


v=(c / n)=(3×10^8 / 1.25)
=2.4×10^8 m/s.


Then,


lambda=(v / f)
=(2.4×10^8 / 5×10^{14)}
=4.8×10^{-7} m
=480 nm.


Using the vacuum speed directly without accounting for the refractive index would give 600 nm, which is incorrect for the wavelength inside the material.

title: Comparing the frequencies of two colours in glass
question: Red light has a wavelength of 700 nm in air, while violet light has a wavelength of 400 nm in air. Both enter the same glass block. What is the ratio f_V:f_R?
explanation:
Frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength in the same initial medium:


(f_V / f_R)=(lambda_R / lambda_V)
=(700 / 400)=frac74.


The frequencies remain unchanged when the two colours enter glass. Their wavelengths decrease by different factors, but their frequency ratio remains 7:4.

title: Photon energy of violet light
question: A violet photon has a frequency of 7.5×10^ Hz. Calculate its energy using h=6.63×10^ J s.
explanation:
Photon energy is


E=hf.


Thus,


E=(6.63×10^{-34})(7.5×10^{14})
=4.9725×10^{-19} J.


Therefore, E≈4.97×10^{-19} J. The energy is proportional to frequency, not wavelength.

title: Rayleigh scattering ratio for two wavelengths
question: Two beams of wavelengths 450 nm and 600 nm pass through the same atmosphere. Assuming Rayleigh scattering, what is the ratio of their scattering intensities, I_:I_, for equal incident intensities and otherwise identical conditions?
explanation:
Rayleigh scattering follows


Iproptofrac1{lambda⁴}.


Therefore,


frac{I_{450}}{I_{600}}
=≤ft((600 / 450)right)⁴
=≤ft(frac43right)⁴
=(256 / 81).


The shorter-wavelength beam is scattered more strongly. The exponent must be four, not two.

title: Travel time of an X-ray pulse through a vacuum
question: An X-ray pulse travels 1.5×10^9 m through vacuum. What is its travel time?
explanation:
t=frac dc
=(1.5×10^9 / 3×10^8)
=5.0 s.


X-rays travel at the same speed as visible light in vacuum. Their higher frequency does not make them travel faster.

title: Minimum deviation: recovering the prism angle
question: A prism produces a minimum deviation of 36^°. At this position, the angle of incidence is 48^°. Find the angle of the prism.
explanation:
At minimum deviation, the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence:


delta_m=2i-A.


Hence,


A=2i-delta_m
=2(48^°)-36^°
=60^°.


The minimum deviation is not equal to the prism angle; it is related to it through the symmetric ray path.

title: Speed and wavelength of infrared radiation in glass
question: Infrared radiation has a wavelength of 1000 nm in air and enters a glass medium of refractive index 1.5. What are its speed and wavelength in glass?

options.text: 2×10^8 m/s, approximately 667 nm

explanation:
The speed is


v=(3×10^8 / 1.5)
=2×10^8 m/s.


The wavelength becomes


lambda_g=(1000 / 1.5)
≈667 nm.


The frequency remains unchanged. Option B incorrectly increases the wavelength in a medium where light travels more slowly.

title: Electromagnetic spectrum: calculating the frequency of a radio wave
question: A radio wave has a wavelength of 150 m in vacuum. Calculate its frequency.
explanation:
f=frac clambda
=(3×10^8 / 150)
=2×10^6 Hz.


The wavelength is very long compared with visible light, so the frequency is much lower.

title: Comparing ultraviolet and visible photon energies
question: A UV photon has a frequency of 1.2×10^ Hz, while a visible-light photon has a frequency of 6×10^ Hz. What is the ratio of their photon energies, E_:E_?

title: Wavelength from photon energy
question: A photon has energy 3.315×10^ J. Taking h=6.63×10^ J s and c=3×10^8 m/s, calculate its wavelength in vacuum.

options.text: 200 nm
400 nm
600 nm
800 nm

explanation:
Using E=hc/lambda,


lambda=(hc / E).



lambda=
frac{(6.63×10^{-34})(3×10^8)}
{3.315×10^{-19}}
=6×10^{-7} m.


Thus, lambda=600 nm, which is within the visible range.

title: Comparing wavelengths inside two media
question: A monochromatic beam has a wavelength of 600 nm in vacuum. It enters medium P with refractive index 1.2, then a separate identical-frequency beam enters medium Q with refractive index 1.5. What is the ratio lambda_P:lambda_Q?
explanation:
For a fixed frequency,


lambda=(lambda₀ / n).


Therefore,


lambda_P=(600 / 1.2)=500 nm


and


lambda_Q=(600 / 1.5)=400 nm.


Hence,


lambda_P:lambda_Q=500:400=5:4.


The medium with the higher refractive index has the shorter wavelength.

title: Deviation in a prism: determining the incidence angle
question: A prism has an angle of 55^°. A ray emerges at 42^° and undergoes a total deviation of 35^°. What is its angle of incidence?
explanation:
The prism relation is


delta=i+e-A.


Therefore,


i=delta+A-e
=35^°+55^°-42^°
=48^°.


The incidence angle is not obtained by subtracting the deviation from the prism angle alone.

title: Comparing electromagnetic frequencies from wavelengths
question: Three electromagnetic waves have wavelengths of 10^ m, 10^ m, and 10^ m, respectively. What is the ratio of their frequencies in the same order?
explanation:
In vacuum,


f=frac clambda.


The frequencies are therefore inversely proportional to the wavelengths:


frac1{10^{-10}}:frac1{10^{-7}}:frac1{10^{-3}}.


Normalising to the smallest frequency gives


10^7:10³:1.


The shortest wavelength corresponds to the highest frequency.

title: Comparing photon energies across the electromagnetic spectrum
question: A gamma-ray photon has a frequency of 3×10^ Hz, while a radio-wave photon has a frequency of 3×10^6 Hz. What is the ratio of their photon energies?

title: Speed of light in a medium from wavelength measurements
question: A beam has a wavelength of 500 nm in air and 400 nm in a transparent material. Assuming its frequency remains unchanged, calculate the speed of light in that material.
explanation:
The refractive index is


n=frac{lambda_{rm air}}{lambda_{rm material}}
=(500 / 400)=1.25.


Thus,


v=frac cn
=(3×10^8 / 1.25)
=2.4×10^8 m/s.


The wavelength falls by a factor of 0.8, so the speed falls by the same factor when the frequency is unchanged.

title: Calculating the scattering-intensity ratio
question: Two wavelengths, 400 nm and 800 nm, pass through the same medium under conditions where Rayleigh scattering applies. For equal incident intensities, what is the scattering-intensity ratio I_:I_?
explanation:
Rayleigh scattering intensity varies as the inverse fourth power of wavelength:


frac{I_{400}}{I_{800}}
=≤ft((800 / 400)right)⁴
=2⁴=16.


The 400 nm beam is scattered 16 times as intensely as the 800 nm beam under the stated conditions.

title: Two-way electromagnetic travel time
question: A radar sends a microwave pulse towards an object 45 km away and receives its reflected pulse. Assuming the pulse travels at 3×10^8 m/s in both directions, what is the total time between transmission and reception?

options.text: 75 μs
150 μs
300 μs
450 μs

explanation:
The pulse travels to the object and back, so the total distance is


d=2(45 km)=90,000 m.


Therefore,


t=(90,000 / 3×10^8)
=3×10^{-4} s
=300 μs.


**Correction check:** The calculated round-trip time is 300 μs, so the correct answer is **C**, not B.

title: Frequency and wavelength of ultraviolet radiation
question: An ultraviolet wave travels through vacuum at 3×10^8 m/s and has a frequency of 1.5×10^ Hz. What is its wavelength?

options.text: 50 nm
200 nm
450 nm

explanation:
Using c=flambda,


lambda=(3×10^8 / 1.5×10^{15)}
=2×10^{-7} m.


Converting to nanometres,


lambda=200 nm.


Option C corresponds to a longer wavelength and therefore a lower frequency at the same wave speed.

title: Comparing the travel times of two electromagnetic signals
question: Two electromagnetic signals travel through vacuum over a distance of 600 km. Signal P is a radio wave with frequency 10^6 Hz, and signal Q is a visible-light wave with frequency 6×10^ Hz. Ignoring delays in the source and detector, what is the difference between their travel times?

options.text: 0 s

explanation:
Both signals are electromagnetic waves travelling through vacuum. Their propagation speed is the same:


c=3×10^8 m/s.


The distance is


d=600 km=6×10^5 m.


For either signal,


t=(6×10^5 / 3×10^8)
=2×10^{-3} s.


Therefore,


Δ t=0.


The frequencies differ enormously, but frequency does not determine the speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum.

title: Speed of red and violet light in glass
question: The refractive indices of a particular glass for red and violet light are 1.50 and 1.54, respectively. Calculate the difference between their speeds in the glass.
explanation:
Using v=c/n,


v_R=(3×10^8 / 1.50)
=2.00×10^8 m/s



v_V=(3×10^8 / 1.54)
≈1.9481×10^8 m/s


Therefore,


Δ v≈5.19×10^6 m/s.


**Correction check:** This evaluates to 5.2×10^6 m/s, so the correct option is **A**, not C.

title: Wavelength in glass when frequency is unchanged
question: A monochromatic beam has a wavelength of 600 nm in air. It enters glass of refractive index 1.5. What is its wavelength in glass and its frequency?

title: Finding the refractive index from the speed of light
question: Light travels through a glass sample at 2.0×10^8 m/s. A second colour travels through the same sample at 1.875×10^8 m/s. Taking the refractive index of air as 1, what is the refractive index of the second colour relative to air?
explanation:
For a transparent medium,


n=(c / v).


Therefore,


n=(3×10^8 / 1.875×10^8)=1.60.


The tempting option C corresponds to the first colour's refractive index, not the second's.

title: Prism deviation from measured angles
question: A ray enters a prism at an angle of incidence 48^° and emerges at an angle of emergence 42^°. The prism angle is 60^°. What is the angle of deviation?
explanation:
For a prism,


delta=i+e-A.


Substituting,


delta=48^°+42^°-60^°
=30^°.


**Correction check:** The calculation gives 30^°, so the correct answer is **A**, not C. This illustrates why the formula must be applied before selecting an option.

title: Determining the prism angle
question: A prism produces a deviation of 38^°. The angles of incidence and emergence are 52^° and 46^°, respectively. What is the prism angle?
explanation:
Using delta=i+e-A,


A=i+e-delta



A=52^°+46^°-38^°
=60^°.


The prism angle is not the sum of the incidence and emergence angles; the deviation must be subtracted.

title: Finding the internal refraction angle
question: A prism has an angle of 60^°. At a particular position, the first internal refraction angle is 24^°. What is the second internal refraction angle?
explanation:
For a prism,


r₁+r₂=A.


Hence,


r₂=60^°-24^°=36^°.


The two internal angles are equal only in the symmetric minimum-deviation position, not for every ray path.

title: Minimum deviation and refractive index
question: A prism has an angle A=60^° and a minimum deviation delta_m=40^°. Calculate its refractive index relative to air.

options.text: dfrac{sin 40^°}{sin 30^°}
dfrac{sin 50^°}{sin 30^°}
dfrac{sin 70^°}{sin 60^°}
dfrac{sin 30^°}{sin 50^°}

explanation:
At minimum deviation,


n=(sin[(A+delta_m)/2] / sin(A/2)).


Therefore,


n=(sin 50^° / sin30^°)
≈(0.7660 / 0.5)
≈1.532.


Option A incorrectly uses the minimum deviation directly in the numerator.

title: Frequency of yellow light
question: Monochromatic yellow light has a wavelength of 500 nm in air. Using c=3×10^8 m/s, calculate its frequency.
explanation:
Convert wavelength into metres:


lambda=500×10^{-9} m.


Then,


f=(c / lambda)
=(3×10^8 / 5×10^{-7)}
=6.0×10^{14} Hz.


Option B results from an incorrect conversion of nanometres to metres.

title: Wavelength of ultraviolet radiation
question: An electromagnetic wave has a frequency of 7.5×10^ Hz. Its wavelength in vacuum is:

options.text: 400 nm
225 nm
750 nm
40 nm

explanation:
lambda=(c / f)
=(3×10^8 / 7.5×10^{14)}
=4.0×10^{-7} m.


Since 1 nm=10^{-9} m,


lambda=400 nm.


The radiation lies near the ultraviolet boundary of the visible spectrum, depending on the wavelength-band convention.

title: Comparing the speeds of two colours
question: The refractive indices of red and violet light in a glass prism are 1.50 and 1.60, respectively. What is the difference between their speeds in glass?
explanation:
v_R=(3×10^8 / 1.50)
=2.0×10^8 m/s



v_V=(3×10^8 / 1.60)
=1.875×10^8 m/s.


Thus,


v_R-v_V=1.25×10^7 m/s.


**Correction check:** The calculation gives 1.25×10^7 m/s, so the correct answer is **A**, not D.

title: Travel time of radio waves
question: A radio signal travels from a spacecraft to a receiving station 1.2×10^8 m away through space. How long does it take to arrive, ignoring processing delays?
explanation:
t=(d / c)
=(1.2×10^8 / 3×10^8)
=0.40 s.


The distance is 40% of a light-second, so the travel time is 0.40 s.

title: Wavelength of a microwave signal
question: A microwave transmitter operates at 10 GHz. What is the wavelength of its radiation in air, taking its speed as 3×10^8 m/s?
explanation:
10 GHz=10^{10} Hz.


Therefore,


lambda=(3×10^8 / 10^{10)}
=3×10^{-2} m
=0.03 m.


**Correction check:** The calculated wavelength is 0.03 m, so the correct answer is **B**, not C.

title: Wavelength change for red light entering glass
question: Red light has a wavelength of 750 nm in air and enters glass of refractive index 1.50. What is its wavelength inside the glass?

options.text: 500 nm
750 nm
250 nm

explanation:
The frequency remains constant and the wavelength decreases by the refractive index:


lambda_g=frac{lambda_{rm air}}{n}
=(750 / 1.50)=500 nm.


The wavelength does not increase to 1125 nm; light travels more slowly in glass than in air.

title: Speed of light in a transparent medium
question: A transparent material has a refractive index of 1.25 for a particular radiation. What is the speed of that radiation inside the material?
explanation:
v=(c / n)
=(3.00×10^8 / 1.25)
=2.40×10^8 m/s.


The speed in an ordinary transparent medium is less than the speed in vacuum.

title: Comparing photon energies using wavelengths
question: Two monochromatic electromagnetic beams have wavelengths of 600 nm and 200 nm in vacuum. What is the ratio of the energy of a photon in the shorter-wavelength beam to that in the longer-wavelength beam?
explanation:
Photon energy is E=hf, and f=c/lambda. Thus, Epropto1/lambda.


frac{E_{200}}{E_{600}}
=(600 / 200)=3.


The 200 nm photon has three times the energy of the 600 nm photon.

title: Light-travel time from the Moon
question: The mean Earth–Moon distance is approximately 3.84×10^8 m. How long does light take to travel this distance in vacuum?
explanation:
t=(d / c)
=(3.84×10^8 / 3×10^8)
=1.28 s.


The distance is approximately 1.28 light-seconds. The common trap is losing a power of ten while dividing.

title: Calculating deviation using incidence and emergence
question: A ray enters a glass prism at 55^° and emerges at 45^°. If the prism angle is 60^°, calculate the total deviation.
explanation:
delta=i+e-A



delta=55^°+45^°-60^°
=40^°.


Adding the two external angles without subtracting the prism angle gives an incorrect result.

title: Refractive index from minimum deviation
question: A glass prism has an angle of 60^° and a minimum deviation of 30^°. What is its refractive index relative to air?
explanation:
n=(sin[(A+delta_m)/2] / sin(A/2))



n=(sin45^° / sin30^°)
=(0.7071 / 0.5)
≈1.414.


**Correction check:** The correct numerical value is approximately 1.414, so the correct answer is **C**, not D.

title: Refraction through a prism: tracing the internal ray
question: A triangular glass prism has its base horizontal. A ray enters the left refracting face, bends towards the normal inside the glass, and then emerges through the right face. The dashed line at the first face is the normal. Which statement correctly explains the ray's behaviour at the first face?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="b21a" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0L6 3L0 6Z" fill="#D97706" /></marker></defs><polygon points="155,20 55,160 255,160" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".17" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M8 100 L115 65 L190 130 L325 85" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.4" marker-end="url(#b21a)" /><path d="M115 65 L145 110" stroke="#64748B" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><text x="14" y="88" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Incident</text><text x="120" y="52" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Normal</text><text x="155" y="151" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Inside glass</text><text x="256" y="70" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Emergent</text></svg>

options.text: It bends away from the normal because glass is optically rarer than air.
It bends towards the normal because it enters a medium of higher refractive index, assuming oblique incidence.
It bends towards the normal because its frequency increases on entering glass.
It travels undeviated at every glass surface, regardless of incidence.

explanation: Light entering glass obliquely from air slows down and bends towards the normal. Its frequency remains unchanged. The bending is caused by the change in wave speed, not by a frequency increase.

title: Colour-dependent deviation: comparing two emergent rays
question: White light passes through an ordinary glass prism. Two rays emerge towards a screen: a red ray R and a violet ray V. Both are measured from the same original incident direction. The diagram exaggerates the separation for clarity. Which comparison is physically correct for ordinary glass?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="100,35 100,135 165,85" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".17" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M10 85 L100 85" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M165 85 L315 85" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M165 85 L310 30" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M165 85 L315 85" stroke="#64748B" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><text x="270" y="75" font-size="12" fill="#DC2626">R</text><text x="270" y="25" font-size="12" fill="#7C3AED">V</text><text x="18" y="73" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">White ray</text><text x="180" y="155" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Screen direction</text></svg>

options.text: delta_R>delta_V, because red has the longer wavelength.
delta_R=delta_V, because both colours enter the same prism.
Violet has the smaller refractive index, so it bends less at both faces.
delta_V>delta_R, because the refractive index of glass is generally greater for violet than for red.

explanation: Normal dispersion means n_V>n_R. Consequently, violet light generally experiences greater net deviation than red light. Using the same prism does not make the deviations equal because the refractive indices depend on wavelength.

title: A glass slab and a prism: comparing emergent directions
question: A ray enters a rectangular glass slab with parallel faces and another ray enters a triangular prism. Both rays enter obliquely from air. The slab's emergent ray is parallel to its incident ray, while the prism's emergent ray is not. Why does the slab generally produce lateral displacement without net angular deviation, while the prism produces angular deviation?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 205" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="25" y="30" width="120" height="62" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M5 75 L60 45 L110 72 L165 42" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /><path d="M5 75 L165 42" stroke="#64748B" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><text x="85" y="20" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Parallel slab</text><polygon points="235,30 185,92 285,92" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M160 56 L205 56 L225 77 L315 125" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" /><text x="235" y="20" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Prism</text><text x="85" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Emergent ray parallel</text><text x="245" y="148" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Net deviation</text><text x="170" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Schematic comparison</text></svg>

options.text: The slab's parallel faces produce equal and opposite angular changes, whereas the prism's non-parallel faces generally do not.
The slab has a refractive index of exactly one, while the prism has a higher refractive index.
The slab absorbs the deviation at its second face, while the prism emits it.
The prism changes the frequency of light, whereas the slab does not.

explanation: In a parallel-sided slab, the second refraction restores the original propagation direction, though the ray is laterally displaced. A prism's refracting faces are not parallel, so the two angular changes do not generally cancel. Neither effect requires a change in frequency.

title: Transparent coloured material versus opaque coloured material
question: White light is incident on two objects. Object P is a transparent green filter, and object Q is an opaque green surface. A detector is placed behind P, while an observer views Q from the illuminated side. Which statement best distinguishes the two objects?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="75" y="28" width="18" height="75" fill="#16A34A" fill-opacity=".5" stroke="#15803D" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="235" y="28" width="45" height="75" fill="#16A34A" stroke="#15803D" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M5 65 L75 65" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M93 65 L145 65" stroke="#16A34A" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M185 65 L235 65" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M235 65 L200 40" stroke="#16A34A" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="84" y="20" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">P: filter</text><text x="257" y="20" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Q: surface</text><text x="35" y="53" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">White</text><text x="112" y="85" font-size="10" fill="#16A34A">Transmitted</text><text x="184" y="125" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Incident</text><text x="201" y="35" font-size="10" fill="#16A34A">Reflected</text><text x="170" y="157" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Different mechanisms determine appearance</text></svg>

options.text: Both must transmit green light because both look green.
The filter reflects only green light, while the opaque surface transmits only green light.
The filter selectively transmits green wavelengths, whereas the opaque surface appears green mainly by reflecting green wavelengths.
Neither object can absorb any visible wavelength.

explanation: A transparent green filter selectively transmits green light and absorbs much of the remaining visible light. An opaque green surface primarily reflects green wavelengths and absorbs much of the rest. The same apparent colour does not imply the same optical mechanism.

title: Two filters in succession
question: White light passes first through a cyan filter, which transmits green and blue light, and then through a yellow filter, which transmits red and green light. The transmitted beams are shown between the filters and after the second filter. Assuming ideal filters and negligible reflection, what colour emerges after both filters?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="65" y="35" width="15" height="80" fill="#06B6D4" fill-opacity=".8" stroke="#0891B2" /><rect x="185" y="35" width="15" height="80" fill="#EAB308" fill-opacity=".8" stroke="#A16207" /><path d="M5 75 L65 75" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M80 75 L185 75" stroke="#16A34A" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M80 83 L185 83" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M200 75 L320 75" stroke="#16A34A" stroke-width="3" /><text x="32" y="62" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">White</text><text x="72" y="25" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Cyan</text><text x="192" y="25" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Yellow</text><text x="130" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">G + B</text><text x="265" y="62" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#16A34A">Green only</text><text x="170" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Ideal selective filters</text></svg>

options.text: White, because two filters always restore the original spectrum.
Green, because green is transmitted by both filters.
Cyan, because the first filter determines the final colour permanently.
Black is guaranteed even if both filters transmit green.

explanation: The cyan filter transmits green and blue. The yellow filter transmits red and green. Only the green component belongs to both transmitted sets, so green emerges. The second filter cannot restore wavelengths removed by the first.

title: Why a blue object can look black in red light
question: A blue opaque object is illuminated by a red lamp. The object reflects blue light efficiently under white illumination but absorbs most red light. An observer views the object from the same side as the lamp. Which explanation is correct?
