diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="130" y="48" width="80" height="62" rx="4" fill="#2563EB" stroke="#1D4ED8" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M15 65 L130 65" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M130 65 L102 42" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><text x="50" y="50" font-size="11" fill="#DC2626">Red lamp</text><text x="170" y="128" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Blue object</text><text x="240" y="63" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Little reflected</text><text x="240" y="76" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">red light</text></svg>

options.text: The object must remain blue because its molecular structure permanently emits blue light.
Red illumination makes every opaque object appear red, regardless of reflectance.
The object becomes transparent when the blue wavelengths are absent.
It appears very dark because the incident red light is mostly absorbed and little blue light is available to reflect.

explanation:
is correct?

A) The object must remain blue because its molecular structure permanently emits blue light.

B) Red illumination makes every opaque object appear red, regardless of reflectance.

C) The object becomes transparent when the blue wavelengths are absent.

D) It appears very dark because the incident red light is mostly absorbed and little blue light is available to reflect.

**Correct Answer: D**

**Reason:** An opaque blue object reflects blue wavelengths present in white light, but under red-only illumination those wavelengths are absent. If the object absorbs red strongly, little light returns to the observer, making it appear nearly black. An object's perceived colour depends on the illumination and its reflectance spectrum.

title: Electromagnetic spectrum: matching radiation to its source
question: Four labelled sources are shown: P is a hot filament, Q is an X-ray tube, R is a radio transmitter, and S is a radioactive nuclear source. The question asks which source-radiation pairing is correctly identified. Which pairing is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" fill="#CBD5E1" fill-opacity=".25"><rect x="12" y="32" width="70" height="65" rx="5" /><rect x="96" y="32" width="70" height="65" rx="5" /><rect x="180" y="32" width="70" height="65" rx="5" /><rect x="264" y="32" width="64" height="65" rx="5" /></g><g font-size="11" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle"><text x="47" y="22">P</text><text x="131" y="22">Q</text><text x="215" y="22">R</text><text x="296" y="22">S</text><text x="47" y="70">Filament</text><text x="131" y="70">X-ray tube</text><text x="215" y="70">Transmitter</text><text x="296" y="70">Nucleus</text></g><path d="M47 100 L47 130 M131 100 L131 130 M215 100 L215 130 M296 100 L296 130" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><g font-size="10" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle"><text x="47" y="146">Thermal</text><text x="131" y="146">High voltage</text><text x="215" y="146">Oscillating current</text><text x="296" y="146">Decay</text></g><text x="170" y="178" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Source identification</text></svg>

options.text: P emits thermal radiation including infrared; Q can produce X-rays when fast electrons strike a target; R produces radio waves; S can emit gamma radiation during nuclear transitions.
P produces only gamma rays; Q produces radio waves; R produces X-rays; S emits only visible light.
P emits infrared only; Q emits gamma rays only; R emits ultraviolet; S emits microwaves only.
Every source produces the same electromagnetic spectrum with equal intensity at all frequencies.

explanation: A hot filament emits a broad thermal spectrum, including visible and infrared radiation. An X-ray tube generates X-rays through electron interactions with a target. Radio transmitters use oscillating electric currents, and nuclear transitions can emit gamma rays. These sources do not produce identical spectra.

title: Infrared radiation and thermal detection
question: An infrared source is directed towards a blackened thermopile. A visible-light screen placed in the same path is not used as the detector. The thermopile produces a measurable signal when the radiation is absorbed. Why is a blackened thermopile appropriate for detecting infrared radiation?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="20" y="45" width="75" height="65" rx="5" fill="#64748B" fill-opacity=".15" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="57" y="72" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">IR</text><text x="57" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">source</text><path d="M95 77 L205 77" stroke="#EA580C" stroke-width="2.7" stroke-dasharray="5 3" /><rect x="205" y="38" width="72" height="78" rx="5" fill="#111827" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="2" /><text x="241" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#FFFFFF">Blackened</text><text x="241" y="83" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#FFFFFF">thermopile</text><path d="M277 77 L312 77 L312 42" fill="none" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="2" /><text x="312" y="31" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Meter</text><text x="170" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Thermal effect of absorbed IR</text></svg>

options.text: Infrared photons have zero energy and must first be converted into visible photons.
A thermopile measures only the frequency of visible light.
Absorbed infrared radiation heats the detector, producing a measurable thermoelectric signal.
Infrared radiation cannot travel through air, so the detector measures only air movement.

explanation: Infrared radiation transfers energy to an absorbing surface, raising its temperature. A thermopile can convert a temperature difference into a voltage signal. Infrared radiation is electromagnetic radiation and can travel through air; it does not require a medium for propagation.

title: Ultraviolet radiation: fluorescence versus heating
question: Two identical samples are exposed separately to ultraviolet radiation. Sample P contains a fluorescent substance that glows visibly, while sample Q is a blackened surface used to investigate heating. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two observations?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="45" y="55" width="85" height="70" rx="8" fill="#A7F3D0" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="210" y="55" width="85" height="70" rx="8" fill="#111827" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M15 88 L45 88 M180 88 L210 88" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="4 3" /><text x="87" y="42" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">P: fluorescent</text><text x="252" y="42" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Q: blackened</text><text x="87" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#065F46">Visible glow</text><text x="87" y="99" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#065F46">possible</text><text x="252" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#FFFFFF">Absorption</text><text x="252" y="99" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#FFFFFF">and heating</text><text x="170" y="151" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Two different detection mechanisms</text></svg>

options.text: Fluorescence proves that ultraviolet radiation has changed into infrared radiation only.
A fluorescent sample may emit visible light after absorbing UV, while a blackened detector can reveal UV energy through heating.
Both samples detect UV only by reflecting it unchanged towards the eye.
Heating can occur only if the incident radiation is visible.

explanation: Fluorescence involves absorption followed by emission of light, often at a longer wavelength. A blackened surface can absorb incident UV energy and convert it into thermal energy. These are different detection mechanisms; neither requires the incident radiation to be visible.

title: X-rays: penetration and absorption
question: A beam of X-rays passes through three materials of increasing effective thickness: paper, a thin aluminium sheet and a thick lead block. Detectors are positioned behind each material. Which conclusion is scientifically sound?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="55" width="40" height="50" fill="#64748B" fill-opacity=".15" stroke="#64748B" /><rect x="100" y="45" width="45" height="70" fill="#94A3B8" fill-opacity=".65" stroke="#64748B" /><rect x="205" y="35" width="50" height="90" fill="#475569" stroke="#334155" /><path d="M50 80 L100 80 M145 80 L205 80 M255 80 L310 80" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="5 3" /><text x="30" y="43" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Paper</text><text x="122" y="32" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Aluminium</text><text x="230" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Lead</text><text x="30" y="135" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">High</text><text x="122" y="135" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Reduced</text><text x="230" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Strongly reduced</text><text x="170" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Qualitative comparison; thickness and energy matter</text></svg>

options.text: All X-rays pass through every material without absorption because they are electromagnetic waves.
Paper must attenuate X-rays more strongly than lead in every possible arrangement.
X-rays are charged particles, so their penetration depends only on electric attraction.
X-rays can penetrate soft materials relatively well, while dense, high-atomic-number materials such as lead can attenuate them strongly; the result depends on energy and thickness.

explanation: X-rays are high-frequency electromagnetic waves. Their attenuation depends on photon energy, material composition and thickness. Lead is commonly used for shielding because it can attenuate X-rays strongly, but no material provides absolute protection under every condition.

title: Radio waves and microwaves: wavelength versus frequency
question: A transmitter sends two electromagnetic signals through air. Signal P has a wavelength of 3 m, while signal Q has a wavelength of 3 cm. The diagram indicates that both travel at approximately the speed of light in air. Which statement correctly compares their frequencies?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 48 Q25 18 40 48 T70 48 T100 48 T130 48 T160 48" fill="none" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2.2" /><path d="M10 110 Q12 90 14 110 T18 110 T22 110 T26 110 T30 110 T34 110 T38 110 T42 110 T46 110 T50 110 T54 110 T58 110 T62 110 T66 110 T70 110 T74 110 T78 110 T82 110 T86 110 T90 110 T94 110 T98 110 T102 110 T106 110 T110 110 T114 110 T118 110 T122 110 T126 110 T130 110 T134 110 T138 110 T142 110 T146 110 T150 110 T154 110 T158 110 T162 110" fill="none" stroke="#EA580C" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="180" y="47" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">P: λ = 3 m</text><text x="180" y="108" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Q: λ = 3 cm</text><text x="170" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Not to scale</text></svg>

options.text: P has 100 times the frequency of Q because its wavelength is longer.
Q has 100 times the frequency of P because its wavelength is 100 times shorter.
Both have identical frequencies because both travel at the speed of light.
Q has one-hundredth the frequency of P because its wavelength is shorter.

explanation:
In air, approximately f=c/lambda. Converting units gives 3 m=300 cm. Hence,


(f_Q / f_P)=(lambda_P / lambda_Q)
=(300 / 3)=100.


Signal Q has 100 times the frequency of P. Equal propagation speeds do not imply equal frequencies when wavelengths differ.

title: Electromagnetic spectrum: comparing photon energies
question: Three monochromatic radiation beams are labelled P, Q and R. Their positions on a spectrum chart correspond respectively to infrared, visible light and ultraviolet radiation. For photons from these three beams, which ordering of energy per photon is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="20" y="45" width="300" height="30" rx="3" fill="#CBD5E1" fill-opacity=".4" stroke="#64748B" /><rect x="20" y="45" width="100" height="30" fill="#EA580C" /><rect x="120" y="45" width="100" height="30" fill="#2563EB" /><rect x="220" y="45" width="100" height="30" fill="#7C3AED" /><text x="70" y="37" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">P</text><text x="170" y="37" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Q</text><text x="270" y="37" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">R</text><text x="70" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#FFFFFF">Infrared</text><text x="170" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#FFFFFF">Visible</text><text x="270" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#FFFFFF">UV</text><path d="M25 97 L315 97" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="25" y="115" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Lower frequency</text><text x="315" y="115" text-anchor="end" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Higher frequency</text><text x="170" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Energy increases with frequency</text></svg>

options.text: E_P>E_Q>E_R
E_P=E_Q=E_R
E_R>E_Q>E_P
E_Q>E_P>E_R

explanation: Photon energy is E=hf. Ultraviolet has a higher frequency than visible light, which has a higher frequency than infrared. Thus E_R>E_Q>E_P. This comparison concerns the energy of each photon, not the total energy carried by a beam.

title: Why danger signals use red light
question: A red warning lamp and a blue warning lamp emit light of comparable initial intensity through a hazy atmosphere containing small suspended particles. An observer is positioned at a distance from both lamps. Why is red commonly used for danger signals intended to be seen from a distance through haze?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="25" width="320" height="105" rx="10" fill="#CBD5E1" fill-opacity=".2" stroke="#94A3B8" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><circle cx="42" cy="57" r="12" fill="#DC2626" /><circle cx="42" cy="100" r="12" fill="#2563EB" /><path d="M54 57 L290 57" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="2.6" /><path d="M54 100 L290 100" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-dasharray="5 4" /><g fill="#64748B"><circle cx="95" cy="45" r="2" /><circle cx="128" cy="73" r="2" /><circle cx="167" cy="44" r="2" /><circle cx="201" cy="88" r="2" /><circle cx="246" cy="48" r="2" /><circle cx="275" cy="113" r="2" /></g><text x="42" y="18" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Sources</text><text x="288" y="42" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Observer</text><text x="170" y="151" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Atmospheric haze (schematic)</text></svg>

options.text: Red has the shortest visible wavelength and is scattered most strongly.
Red light cannot be absorbed by atmospheric particles under any conditions.
Red has the highest frequency of all visible colours, so it always travels fastest in air.
Red generally undergoes less Rayleigh scattering than shorter visible wavelengths, helping preserve the direct beam through haze, although visibility also depends on other conditions.

explanation: Rayleigh scattering is weaker for longer wavelengths. Red light is therefore scattered less than blue light by sufficiently small atmospheric molecules, helping it remain prominent over distance. Real haze can also involve larger particles, absorption and contrast effects, so red is not immune to attenuation.

title: Electromagnetic waves in vacuum
question: A vacuum chamber contains an electromagnetic-wave source and detector separated by a fixed distance. A second diagram shows a sound source and microphone in the same evacuated chamber. What should happen when the chamber is sufficiently evacuated?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="28" width="316" height="52" rx="7" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".12" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="12" y="102" width="316" height="52" rx="7" fill="#CBD5E1" fill-opacity=".2" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="25" y="43" width="45" height="22" fill="#64748B" fill-opacity=".25" stroke="#64748B" /><rect x="270" y="43" width="45" height="22" fill="#64748B" fill-opacity=".25" stroke="#64748B" /><path d="M70 54 L270 54" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="5 3" /><rect x="25" y="117" width="45" height="22" fill="#64748B" fill-opacity=".25" stroke="#64748B" /><rect x="270" y="117" width="45" height="22" fill="#64748B" fill-opacity=".25" stroke="#64748B" /><path d="M70 128 L270 128" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="2 5" /><text x="170" y="19" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Electromagnetic wave</text><text x="170" y="95" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Sound wave</text><text x="170" y="171" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Vacuum chamber</text></svg>

options.text: Both signals propagate unchanged because every wave can travel through a vacuum.
The electromagnetic signal can reach the detector, but ordinary sound cannot propagate through the vacuum.
Sound travels at 3×10^8 m/s after the air is removed.
Electromagnetic waves require air molecules to transfer energy between the source and detector.

explanation: Electromagnetic waves can propagate through vacuum at approximately 3×10^8 m/s. Sound is a mechanical wave requiring a material medium. Evacuating the chamber therefore prevents ordinary sound propagation but does not prevent electromagnetic transmission.

title: Electromagnetic spectrum: identifying the radiation from wavelength
question: A detector measures radiation with a wavelength of 10^ m. Its position on a spectrum chart is between ultraviolet and gamma rays, within the X-ray region for the stated wavelength. Which conclusion is best?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="15" y="40" width="310" height="30" fill="#CBD5E1" fill-opacity=".3" stroke="#64748B" /><rect x="68" y="40" width="62" height="30" fill="#6366F1" fill-opacity=".7" stroke="#4F46E5" /><path d="M99 15 L99 39" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="2" /><text x="99" y="11" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">10⁻¹⁰ m</text><g font-size="10" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle"><text x="38" y="88">Gamma</text><text x="99" y="88">X-rays</text><text x="160" y="88">UV</text><text x="220" y="88">Visible</text><text x="286" y="88">IR / longer</text></g><text x="170" y="121" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Schematic; band boundaries are approximate</text></svg>

options.text: The radiation is an X-ray; its frequency in vacuum is approximately 3×10^{18} Hz.
The radiation is visible violet light because all short wavelengths are visible.
The radiation is a radio wave because its wavelength is expressed in metres.
The radiation is an infrared wave because it has lower energy than visible light.

explanation:
Using f=c/lambda,


f=(3×10^8 / 10^{-10)}
=3×10^{18} Hz.


This wavelength lies in the X-ray region. The unit metre is used for all wavelengths; the numerical value, not the unit alone, identifies the region.

title: Infrared, ultraviolet and visible radiation: common properties
question: Three beams labelled P, Q and R represent infrared, visible light and ultraviolet radiation, respectively. They pass through the same vacuum chamber towards detectors, with no material barrier between source and detector. Which property is shared by all three radiations?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="25" width="316" height="105" rx="8" fill="#CBD5E1" fill-opacity=".15" stroke="#64748B" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><g stroke-width="2.5"><path d="M25 50 L310 50" stroke="#EA580C" /><path d="M25 78 L310 78" stroke="#2563EB" /><path d="M25 106 L310 106" stroke="#7C3AED" /></g><g font-size="11" fill="currentColor"><text x="28" y="42">P: IR</text><text x="28" y="70">Q: Visible</text><text x="28" y="98">R: UV</text><text x="300" y="42" text-anchor="end">Detector</text></g><text x="170" y="146" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">All three are electromagnetic waves</text></svg>

options.text: All are visible to the unaided human eye.
All have identical frequencies and wavelengths.
All are transverse electromagnetic waves that travel at 3×10^8 m/s in vacuum.
All require a material medium and cannot propagate through vacuum.

explanation: Infrared, visible and ultraviolet radiation are all electromagnetic waves. In vacuum they travel at the same speed, c, but they have different frequencies and wavelengths. Only the visible portion is ordinarily detectable by the unaided eye.

title: Scattering versus refraction at a glass boundary
question: A narrow beam of white light reaches a clean glass prism in arrangement P. In arrangement Q, the beam passes through a colloidal suspension, where its path is visible from the side due to scattered light. Which comparison is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="82" y="20" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">P: Prism</text><text x="255" y="20" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Q: Colloid</text><polygon points="70,42 30,110 110,110" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M5 85 L55 85 L83 98 L140 68" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.3" /><rect x="195" y="42" width="115" height="83" rx="6" fill="#93C5FD" fill-opacity=".2" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M175 82 L310 82" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="2.3" /><path d="M235 82 L215 58 M248 82 L265 53 M260 82 L280 108 M232 82 L210 110" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><g fill="#64748B"><circle cx="225" cy="62" r="2" /><circle cx="260" cy="99" r="2" /><circle cx="280" cy="65" r="2" /><circle cx="215" cy="95" r="2" /></g><text x="82" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Direction changes</text><text x="252" y="143" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Light scattered sideways</text><text x="170" y="174" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Two distinct optical effects</text></svg>

options.text: Refraction and scattering are identical because both always produce seven separate colours.
Refraction changes the direction of a ray at a boundary due to a change in wave speed; scattering redirects light through interactions with particles or inhomogeneities.
Scattering occurs only in a vacuum, while refraction occurs only in solids.
Refraction requires absorption and re-emission of every photon, whereas scattering never changes a light ray's direction.

explanation: Refraction occurs when light changes propagation direction because its speed changes across a boundary. Scattering redirects light through interactions with particles or variations in a medium. Scattering may make a beam visible from the side, whereas a clean prism produces refraction and wavelength-dependent deviation.

title: A rainbow and the observer's line of sight
question: A primary rainbow is observed when sunlight comes from behind the observer. Light from raindrops in front of the observer reaches the eye after refraction, dispersion and one internal reflection. The antisolar direction points away from the Sun, through the observer. Which statement correctly describes the viewing geometry of a primary rainbow?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 195" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="30" cy="40" r="14" fill="#FBBF24" stroke="#D97706" /><path d="M45 40 L115 70" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="2.3" /><circle cx="170" cy="95" r="7" fill="#64748B" /><path d="M170 95 L295 95" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4" /><circle cx="285" cy="95" r="8" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".4" stroke="#2563EB" /><path d="M285 95 L175 95" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2.3" /><path d="M170 95 L170 35" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><path d="M165 43 A52 52 0 0 1 175 43" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="2.3" fill="none" /><text x="28" y="65" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Sun</text><text x="170" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Observer</text><text x="285" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Drop</text><text x="230" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Antisolar direction</text><text x="170" y="157" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Rainbow geometry (schematic)</text></svg>

options.text: The Sun must be directly in front of the observer, and the rainbow forms around the Sun.
A rainbow is seen only when the observer looks straight at the Sun through a raindrop.
Every raindrop sends all seven colours into the observer's eye simultaneously at the same angle.
The Sun is generally behind the observer, and raindrops in the opposite part of the sky send particular colours towards the observer at characteristic angles around the antisolar direction.

explanation: A primary rainbow appears opposite the Sun, centred on the antisolar direction. Individual raindrops send different colours towards the observer at different characteristic angles. The rainbow is therefore an angular phenomenon involving the observer, the Sun and many droplets—not a coloured object fixed at one location in the sky.

title: Continuous spectrum versus line spectrum
question: Two spectral records are displayed. Record P shows a continuous band of colours with no dark gaps. Record Q shows separate bright lines against a dark background. Which inference is justified by these records alone?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="170" y="18" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Spectral records</text><rect x="20" y="35" width="300" height="35" rx="3" fill="#DC2626" /><rect x="20" y="35" width="43" height="35" fill="#7C3AED" /><rect x="63" y="35" width="43" height="35" fill="#4F46E5" /><rect x="106" y="35" width="43" height="35" fill="#2563EB" /><rect x="149" y="35" width="43" height="35" fill="#16A34A" /><rect x="192" y="35" width="43" height="35" fill="#EAB308" /><rect x="235" y="35" width="43" height="35" fill="#F97316" /><text x="20" y="29" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">P</text><rect x="20" y="100" width="300" height="35" rx="3" fill="#111827" /><g fill="#E5E7EB"><rect x="48" y="100" width="4" height="35" /><rect x="91" y="100" width="3" height="35" /><rect x="147" y="100" width="5" height="35" /><rect x="210" y="100" width="3" height="35" /><rect x="278" y="100" width="5" height="35" /></g><text x="20" y="94" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Q</text><text x="170" y="157" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Schematic spectra</text></svg>

options.text: P is continuous and Q is a line spectrum; P necessarily has a higher maximum frequency than Q.
Q must come from a hot solid because bright lines are the defining feature of solids.
P is continuous across the represented band, whereas Q contains emission at particular wavelengths; the diagrams alone do not identify the exact source materials.
Both records are identical spectra because all visible wavelengths travel at the same speed in vacuum.

explanation: A continuous spectrum contains a continuous range of wavelengths, while a line spectrum contains distinct wavelengths. The diagrams identify the spectral forms but do not, by themselves, determine the precise source or prove which spectrum has the higher maximum frequency.

title: Electromagnetic spectrum: identifying a harmful exposure
question: A diagram compares three radiation sources. P is an ultraviolet lamp, Q is an X-ray imaging source, and R is an infrared heat lamp. The diagram marks the skin or tissue exposed to each source. Which statement correctly matches the radiation with a possible harmful effect?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 185" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5"><rect x="12" y="28" width="96" height="112" rx="6" fill="#CBD5E1" fill-opacity=".18" /><rect x="122" y="28" width="96" height="112" rx="6" fill="#CBD5E1" fill-opacity=".18" /><rect x="232" y="28" width="96" height="112" rx="6" fill="#CBD5E1" fill-opacity=".18" /></g><g font-size="11" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle"><text x="60" y="19">P: UV</text><text x="170" y="19">Q: X-rays</text><text x="280" y="19">R: Infrared</text></g><path d="M25 65 L94 65" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M135 65 L204 65" stroke="#6366F1" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M245 65 L314 65" stroke="#EA580C" stroke-width="2.5" /><rect x="35" y="90" width="50" height="25" rx="4" fill="#FCA5A5" stroke="#DC2626" /><rect x="145" y="90" width="50" height="25" rx="4" fill="#FCA5A5" stroke="#DC2626" /><rect x="255" y="90" width="50" height="25" rx="4" fill="#FCA5A5" stroke="#DC2626" /><text x="60" y="129" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Skin</text><text x="170" y="129" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Tissue</text><text x="280" y="129" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Skin</text><text x="170" y="162" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Different mechanisms of harm</text></svg>

options.text: UV can damage skin and eyes; X-rays can ionise tissue and damage cells; intense infrared exposure can cause heating and burns.
Only infrared can damage living tissue because UV and X-rays carry no energy.
X-rays are harmless whenever the exposure is invisible, while visible light is always more damaging.
UV, X-rays and infrared produce identical biological effects because they all travel at the same speed in vacuum.

explanation: Ultraviolet radiation can cause skin damage and eye injury. X-rays are ionising radiation and can damage cells and DNA. Infrared radiation primarily produces heating and can cause burns at sufficiently high exposure. The speed shared by electromagnetic waves in vacuum does not mean they have equal photon energies or identical biological effects.

title: Prism illuminated by monochromatic light
question: A prism is illuminated by a narrow beam of monochromatic green light. The emergent beam is shown bending towards the base of the prism, with no fan of colours on the screen. Which statement is correct?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 185" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<defs><marker id="q16arr" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6Z" fill="#16A34A"/></marker></defs>
<polygon points="155,25 75,145 235,145" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2"/>
<path d="M12 75 L125 75 L164 116 L300 116" fill="none" stroke="#16A34A" stroke-width="2.7" markerEnd="url(#q16arr)"/>

<text x="312" y="104" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Screen</text>
<text x="155" y="166" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Single-colour beam</text>
</svg>

options.text: The prism can deviate the green beam, but it will not produce a seven-colour spectrum from ideal monochromatic incident light.
The prism cannot refract green light because dispersion requires white light.
The green beam must split into red and violet because every glass prism creates all seven colours.
The prism changes green light into white light by increasing its frequency.

explanation: Refraction and deviation occur even for monochromatic light. Dispersion separates different wavelengths already present in a beam; it does not create the missing wavelengths. A monochromatic green beam therefore emerges as green, although its direction changes.

title: Additive mixing of primary colours
question: Three coloured spotlights overlap on a white screen. The red and green beams overlap at P, green and blue at Q, and blue and red at R. All three overlap at the central point O. At the central overlap O, all three primary lights have equal intensity. Which result is expected under ideal additive colour mixing?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 205" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect x="10" y="10" width="330" height="175" rx="10" fill="#F8FAFC" stroke="#CBD5E1"/>
<circle cx="140" cy="83" r="52" fill="#EF4444" fill-opacity=".65"/>
<circle cx="210" cy="83" r="52" fill="#22C55E" fill-opacity=".65"/>
<circle cx="175" cy="128" r="52" fill="#3B82F6" fill-opacity=".65"/>
<g font-size="11" fill="#111827" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle"><text x="110" y="40">Red</text><text x="240" y="40">Green</text><text x="175" y="176">Blue</text></g>
<g font-size="11" fill="#111827" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle"><text x="175" y="75">Yellow</text><text x="145" y="123">Magenta</text><text x="205" y="123">Cyan</text><text x="175" y="105">O</text></g>
</svg>

options.text: Black, because the three primary colours cancel each other.
Yellow, because red and green are the only colours that contribute to the centre.
White, because suitably balanced red, green and blue light combine to produce white.
Violet, because blue light has the greatest frequency of the three.

explanation: Red, green and blue are the primary colours of additive light mixing. When suitably balanced and superposed, they produce white light. Red plus green alone produces yellow, not white; additive mixing is different from mixing coloured pigments.

title: Complementary colours in additive mixing
question: A diagram shows white light represented by three additive primary components: red, green and blue. A cyan beam, consisting of green and blue light, is combined with a separate red beam. Why are red and cyan complementary colours in additive mixing?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect x="18" y="40" width="80" height="65" rx="6" fill="#06B6D4" fill-opacity=".8"/>
<rect x="125" y="40" width="80" height="65" rx="6" fill="#EF4444" fill-opacity=".85"/>
<path d="M98 72 L120 72 M205 72 L245 72" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="2.5"/>
<path d="M238 65 L247 72 L238 79" fill="none" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="2.5"/>
<rect x="247" y="40" width="85" height="65" rx="6" fill="#F8FAFC" stroke="#94A3B8"/>
<text x="58" y="69" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#111827">Cyan</text><text x="58" y="84" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#111827">G + B</text>
<text x="165" y="77" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#111827">Red</text>
<text x="289" y="77" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#111827">White</text>
<text x="175" y="135" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Complementary additive colours</text>
</svg>

options.text: Cyan absorbs red light, so their combination always produces black.
Cyan contains green and blue; adding red supplies all three primary components and can produce white light when suitably balanced.
Red and cyan have identical wavelengths but different amplitudes.
Cyan is a monochromatic colour that changes its frequency to red when combined.

explanation: Cyan is formed by adding green and blue light. Red plus cyan therefore supplies red, green and blue components. With suitable relative intensities, the combined light appears white. Complementarity in additive mixing does not mean that one colour absorbs the other.

title: Speed, frequency and wavelength of light in glass
question: A red light beam and a violet light beam enter the same ordinary glass block from air. The diagram shows the violet ray refracted more strongly, with both beams emerging parallel to their respective incident directions from the parallel-sided block. For ordinary glass under normal dispersion, which comparison between red and violet light is correct?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 195" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect x="85" y="30" width="180" height="130" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".15" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2"/>
<path d="M15 65 L85 65 L265 65 L330 65" fill="none" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="2.2"/>
<path d="M15 110 L85 110 L265 110 L330 110" fill="none" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2.2"/>
<path d="M85 65 L265 65 M85 110 L265 110" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 4"/>
<text x="32" y="53" font-size="11" fill="#DC2626">Red</text><text x="32" y="98" font-size="11" fill="#7C3AED">Violet</text>
<text x="175" y="23" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Ordinary glass</text>
<text x="175" y="181" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Parallel-sided block (schematic)</text>
</svg>

options.text: Violet has a lower frequency and a longer wavelength in glass.
Red and violet have equal wavelengths in glass because both travel through the same material.
Violet has a higher frequency in glass because its speed decreases.
Violet has a higher refractive index and lower speed in glass; its frequency remains unchanged at the boundary, so its wavelength in glass is shorter than red's.

explanation: For ordinary glass, n_V>n_R. Since v=c/n, violet travels more slowly than red. Frequency remains fixed at refraction, and lambda=v/f; therefore, violet has the shorter wavelength in glass. A change of speed does not imply a change of frequency.

title: Reading a deviation-versus-incidence graph
question: A graph plots the angle of deviation delta on the vertical axis against the angle of incidence i on the horizontal axis for a prism. The curve decreases, reaches a unique minimum at point M, and then increases. Which interpretation of point M is correct?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 215" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<defs><marker id="q20axis" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6Z" fill="#64748B"/></marker></defs>
<path d="M45 175 L45 25 M45 175 L325 175" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.6" markerEnd="url(#q20axis)"/>
<path d="M70 55 Q175 215 290 55" fill="none" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2.5"/>
<circle cx="180" cy="129" r="4" fill="#DC2626"/>
<path d="M180 129 L180 175" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/>
<path d="M45 129 L180 129" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/>
<text x="32" y="25" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">δ</text><text x="329" y="190" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">i</text>
<text x="188" y="120" font-size="12" fill="#DC2626">M</text>
<text x="180" y="198" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Incidence at minimum deviation</text>

options.text: It represents minimum deviation, where the ray path is symmetric and the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence.
It represents zero refraction, because the prism ceases to affect the ray.
It represents the maximum possible deviation, where the ray travels along the prism base.
It proves that the angle of incidence and the angle of deviation are always equal.

explanation: The minimum point of the deviation-versus-incidence curve represents the minimum deviation position. At this point, the ray path is symmetric, so i=e and r₁=r₂=A/2. The deviation remains non-zero for an ordinary glass prism in air, and it is not generally equal to the incidence angle.

title: Refraction through a prism: identifying the deviation
question: A triangular glass prism has its apex pointing upward and its base horizontal. A white ray enters the left face and emerges from the right face. The incident and emergent rays, when extended, make an angle delta. Which statement correctly describes the angle of deviation delta?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="q1arr" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D97706" /></marker></defs><polygon points="170,28 75,165 265,165" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.18" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M18 85 L112 85" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" marker-end="url(#q1arr)" /><path d="M112 85 L190 135 L310 85" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" marker-end="url(#q1arr)" /><path d="M18 85 L310 85" stroke="#64748B" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="1.4" /><path d="M275 85 A35 35 0 0 1 277 97" fill="none" stroke="#64748B" /><text x="25" y="73" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Incident ray</text><text x="211" y="151" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Emergent ray</text><text x="278" y="76" font-size="13" fill="currentColor">δ</text><text x="171" y="20" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Apex</text><text x="170" y="182" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Base</text></svg>

options.text: It is the angle between the incident ray and the normal at the first face.
It is the angle between the two refracting faces.
It is the angle between the original direction of the incident ray and the emergent ray.
It is always equal to twice the angle of incidence.

explanation: Deviation is the net angular change between the original direction of the incident ray and the emergent ray. The prism angle A is instead the angle between its refracting faces. Deviation is not generally 2i; it depends on incidence, prism geometry and refractive index.

title: Angle of a prism versus angle of deviation
question: A triangular prism is shown with its apex angle marked 60^°. A ray passes through it, and the total deviation is marked 40^°. A student claims that because the prism angle is 60^°, the ray must deviate by 60^°. Which conclusion is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="q2arr" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D97706" /></marker></defs><polygon points="170,25 75,160 265,160" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M10 75 L112 75 L188 119 L322 75" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.3" marker-end="url(#q2arr)" /><path d="M10 75 L322 75" stroke="#64748B" stroke-dasharray="5 4" /><path d="M150 53 A24 24 0 0 1 190 53" fill="none" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="170" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">A = 60°</text><text x="265" y="65" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">δ = 40°</text><text x="18" y="65" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Incident</text><text x="235" y="143" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Emergent</text></svg>

options.text: The claim is incorrect because A and delta represent different angles; the stated deviation is 40^°.
The claim is correct because deviation always equals the prism angle.
The claim is correct only for violet light.
The deviation must be 100^°, the sum of the two marked angles.

explanation: The prism angle A is a geometrical property of the prism, while delta describes the ray's change in direction. They are not generally equal. The given values 60^° and 40^° can coexist.

title: Dispersion: determining the colour order on a screen
question: A narrow beam of white light enters a glass prism. A screen is placed beyond the prism. The diagram shows the upper and lower limits of the emerging fan of colours. Which interpretation of the spectrum is correct for an ordinary glass prism in air?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 220" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="105,55 105,165 190,110" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M15 110 L105 110" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M151 110 L285 45" stroke="#8B5CF6" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M151 110 L285 62" stroke="#4F46E5" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M151 110 L285 79" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M151 110 L285 96" stroke="#16A34A" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M151 110 L285 113" stroke="#EAB308" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M151 110 L285 130" stroke="#F97316" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M151 110 L285 147" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="2" /><rect x="285" y="30" width="5" height="135" fill="#64748B" /><text x="296" y="47" font-size="11" fill="#8B5CF6">V</text><text x="296" y="64" font-size="11" fill="#4F46E5">I</text><text x="296" y="81" font-size="11" fill="#2563EB">B</text><text x="296" y="98" font-size="11" fill="#16A34A">G</text><text x="296" y="115" font-size="11" fill="#A16207">Y</text><text x="296" y="132" font-size="11" fill="#EA580C">O</text><text x="296" y="149" font-size="11" fill="#DC2626">R</text><text x="65" y="101" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">White light</text><text x="226" y="19" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Screen</text><text x="142" y="189" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Prism base below apex</text></svg>

options.text: Red is at the more-deviated end because it has the greatest wavelength.
Violet is least deviated because it travels fastest in glass.
All colours deviate equally, but the screen separates them by frequency.
Violet is more deviated than red because glass generally has a higher refractive index for violet light.

explanation: Ordinary glass has a higher refractive index for violet than for red. Violet therefore travels more slowly in glass and is generally deviated more. Red is deviated least. The resulting order from the most-deviated end to the least-deviated end is VIBGYOR.

title: Identifying the condition for minimum deviation
question: A ray passes symmetrically through a prism. The internal ray makes equal angles with the normals at the two faces, and the incident and emergent rays are symmetric about the prism. Which condition must hold when the prism is in the position of minimum deviation?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 205" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="q4arr" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D97706" /></marker></defs><polygon points="170,25 75,165 265,165" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M10 75 L112 75 L170 126 L228 75 L330 75" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.3" marker-end="url(#q4arr)" /><path d="M112 75 L170 126 L228 75" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.3" /><path d="M112 75 L148 25 M228 75 L192 25" stroke="#64748B" stroke-dasharray="4 3" /><text x="65" y="63" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">i</text><text x="262" y="63" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">e</text><text x="170" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Symmetric ray path</text></svg>

options.text: The angle of incidence is zero.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence, and the refraction angles inside the prism are equal.
The emergent ray travels along the base of the prism.
The refractive index becomes equal to one.

explanation: At minimum deviation, the ray path through the prism is symmetric: i=e and r₁=r₂=A/2. The incidence angle is not generally zero, and the refractive index of glass does not become one.

title: Recombination of the spectrum using a second prism
question: The first glass prism disperses white light into VIBGYOR. A second identical prism is inverted relative to the first and placed in the path of the spectrum so that the colours can recombine. The emergent beam from the second prism is approximately white. Which explanation is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 210" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="80,50 80,145 150,98" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".2" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="235,50 305,98 235,145" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".2" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M10 98 L80 98" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M150 98 L235 65" stroke="#8B5CF6" stroke-width="1.8" /><path d="M150 98 L235 75" stroke="#4F46E5" stroke-width="1.8" /><path d="M150 98 L235 85" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="1.8" /><path d="M150 98 L235 95" stroke="#16A34A" stroke-width="1.8" /><path d="M150 98 L235 105" stroke="#EAB308" stroke-width="1.8" /><path d="M150 98 L235 115" stroke="#F97316" stroke-width="1.8" /><path d="M150 98 L235 125" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="1.8" /><path d="M305 98 L340 98" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="3" /><text x="115" y="30" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Prism 1</text><text x="270" y="30" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Prism 2</text><text x="45" y="87" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">White</text><text x="320" y="87" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">White</text><text x="175" y="160" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Dispersed colours</text><text x="175" y="183" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Second prism opposes dispersion</text></svg>

options.text: The second prism absorbs six colours and transmits only red.
The second prism converts every colour into violet.
The second prism produces an equal and opposite angular separation of the colours, allowing them to overlap again.
The first prism changes the frequency of each colour, and the second restores the original frequencies.

explanation:
is correct?

A) The second prism absorbs six colours and transmits only red.

B) The second prism converts every colour into violet.

C) The second prism produces an equal and opposite angular separation of the colours, allowing them to overlap again.

D) The first prism changes the frequency of each colour, and the second restores the original frequencies.

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:** The inverted second prism produces dispersion in the opposite sense. With a suitable arrangement, the separated colours overlap to form white light again. Neither prism changes the frequency of light during refraction.

title: Newton’s disc: interpreting the experiment
question: A circular disc is divided into seven sectors coloured violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. An arrow indicates rapid rotation about its central axis. After the disc rotates sufficiently rapidly, it appears nearly white or pale grey. Which conclusion is most accurate?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g transform="translate(125 95)"><path d="M0 0 L0 -70 A70 70 0 0 1 54.7 -43.7 Z" fill="#8B5CF6" stroke="white" stroke-width="1" /><path d="M0 0 L54.7 -43.7 A70 70 0 0 1 68.3 15.6 Z" fill="#4F46E5" stroke="white" stroke-width="1" /><path d="M0 0 L68.3 15.6 A70 70 0 0 1 30.4 63.1 Z" fill="#2563EB" stroke="white" stroke-width="1" /><path d="M0 0 L30.4 63.1 A70 70 0 0 1 -30.4 63.1 Z" fill="#16A34A" stroke="white" stroke-width="1" /><path d="M0 0 L-30.4 63.1 A70 70 0 0 1 -68.3 15.6 Z" fill="#EAB308" stroke="white" stroke-width="1" /><path d="M0 0 L-68.3 15.6 A70 70 0 0 1 -54.7 -43.7 Z" fill="#F97316" stroke="white" stroke-width="1" /><path d="M0 0 L-54.7 -43.7 A70 70 0 0 1 0 -70 Z" fill="#DC2626" stroke="white" stroke-width="1" /><circle r="5" fill="#475569" /></g><path d="M225 48 Q265 82 240 117" fill="none" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M232 109 L240 119 L246 107" fill="none" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="247" y="72" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Rapid</text><text x="247" y="85" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">rotation</text><text x="125" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Seven-colour disc</text></svg>

options.text: The colours physically turn into white pigments during rotation.
The eye integrates the rapidly changing colour stimuli, producing an approximately white or grey perception.
Rotation increases the frequency of every colour until it enters the ultraviolet region.
The disc proves that white light is a monochromatic radiation.

explanation: Rapid rotation causes the colour sectors to be perceived together because of temporal integration in vision. Their combined appearance is approximately white or grey, depending on the pigments, illumination and disc design. White light is not monochromatic.

title: Colour of an opaque object under coloured illumination
question: A red opaque object is illuminated only by green light. The reflected light reaching the observer is shown as a separate arrow. Assuming the red object reflects red light strongly but absorbs most green light, how will it appear under this illumination?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="q7g" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6Z" fill="#16A34A" /></marker><marker id="q7r" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6Z" fill="#DC2626" /></marker></defs><rect x="125" y="55" width="80" height="65" rx="5" fill="#DC2626" stroke="#991B1B" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M15 45 L125 70" stroke="#16A34A" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#q7g)" /><path d="M205 70 L290 30" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4" /><text x="18" y="32" font-size="11" fill="#16A34A">Green illumination</text><text x="214" y="92" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Reflected light</text><text x="165" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Red opaque object</text><text x="290" y="22" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Observer</text></svg>

options.text: Bright red, because its colour is fixed regardless of illumination.
White, because green light is a primary colour.
Green, because opaque objects always reflect the incident colour.
Very dark or nearly black, because little green light is reflected to the observer.

explanation: An opaque object can reflect only the wavelengths present in the incident light. Under green-only illumination, the red object has little red light available to reflect and absorbs most of the green light, so it appears dark. Its appearance depends on both its reflectance and the illuminating spectrum.

title: A colour filter and the spectrum incident on it
question: White light falls on a red transmitting filter. The transmitted beam enters a prism, which separates the transmitted light into its component wavelengths. Which result is expected if the filter transmits red light and absorbs the other visible colours effectively?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="115,35 115,135 175,85" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><rect x="75" y="48" width="10" height="75" fill="#DC2626" fill-opacity=".7" stroke="#991B1B" /><path d="M10 85 L75 85" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M85 85 L115 85" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M175 85 L320 85" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="3" /><text x="35" y="73" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">White</text><text x="80" y="34" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Red filter</text><text x="142" y="24" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Prism</text><text x="247" y="70" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Red transmitted</text><text x="247" y="104" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">No full VIBGYOR fan</text></svg>

options.text: The prism produces a complete VIBGYOR spectrum with equal intensities.
The filter itself disperses white light into seven separate beams.
The transmitted beam is predominantly red, so the prism cannot produce the usual full visible spectrum from it.
The red filter changes red light into violet light before it reaches the prism.

explanation: The filter removes most of the non-red components before the light reaches the prism. The prism can refract the transmitted red light, but a nearly monochromatic red beam does not produce the usual seven-colour spectrum. A filter selects wavelengths; it does not create the missing colours.

title: Rayleigh scattering: why the sky appears blue
question: Sunlight enters the atmosphere. Shorter-wavelength blue light is scattered in several directions by small atmospheric molecules, while a larger fraction of the longer-wavelength red light continues approximately forward. For particles much smaller than the wavelength, Rayleigh scattering intensity varies approximately as 1/lambda⁴. If the wavelength of one beam is half that of another, with all other relevant conditions equal, the ratio of their scattering intensities is:
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 195" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="q9arr" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6Z" fill="#D97706" /></marker></defs><circle cx="25" cy="45" r="16" fill="#FBBF24" stroke="#D97706" /><rect x="70" y="15" width="250" height="150" rx="12" fill="#93C5FD" fill-opacity=".15" stroke="#60A5FA" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><path d="M43 45 L150 80 L315 80" fill="none" stroke="#DC2626" stroke-width="2.4" marker-end="url(#q9arr)" /><path d="M150 80 L112 35 M150 80 L205 35 M150 80 L205 125 M150 80 L105 130" fill="none" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2.4" /><circle cx="150" cy="80" r="4" fill="#64748B" /><text x="16" y="76" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Sun</text><text x="220" y="69" font-size="11" fill="#DC2626">Red: forward</text><text x="210" y="147" font-size="11" fill="#2563EB">Blue: scattered</text><text x="190" y="177" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Atmospheric molecules</text></svg>

options.text: 16:1, shorter wavelength to longer wavelength.
8:1, shorter wavelength to longer wavelength.
4:1, shorter wavelength to longer wavelength.
2:1, shorter wavelength to longer wavelength.

explanation:
Since Ipropto 1/lambda⁴,


frac{I_{short}}{I_{long}}
=≤ft(frac{lambda_{long}}{lambda_{short}}right)⁴
=≤ft(frac{2lambda_{short}}{lambda_{short}}right)⁴
=16.


Thus the shorter wavelength is scattered 16 times as intensely under the stated approximation. The exponent is four, not two.

title: Sunrise and sunset: the geometry of red sunlight
question: Two parallel bundles of sunlight enter the atmosphere. At noon, sunlight follows a relatively short atmospheric path; at sunset, sunlight travels through a much longer path before reaching an observer near the horizon. Why does the Sun often appear reddish near the horizon?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 210" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="q10sun" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6Z" fill="#F59E0B" /></marker></defs><path d="M15 170 Q175 130 335 170" fill="none" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M15 160 Q175 120 335 160" fill="none" stroke="#60A5FA" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><circle cx="30" cy="43" r="13" fill="#FBBF24" /><circle cx="30" cy="115" r="13" fill="#FBBF24" /><path d="M44 43 L175 43 L175 140" fill="none" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="2.4" marker-end="url(#q10sun)" /><path d="M44 115 L300 155" fill="none" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="2.4" marker-end="url(#q10sun)" /><path d="M175 43 L190 58 M175 43 L160 58" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M230 144 L250 151 M230 144 L235 128" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="2" /><text x="65" y="28" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Near noon</text><text x="65" y="100" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Sunset</text><text x="195" y="32" font-size="10" fill="#2563EB">Shorter path</text><text x="245" y="120" font-size="10" fill="#2563EB">Longer path</text><text x="175" y="195" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Curved Earth surface and atmosphere (schematic)</text></svg>

options.text: Red light has the highest frequency and is therefore refracted most by air.
The long atmospheric path preferentially scatters shorter visible wavelengths out of the direct beam, leaving relatively more red and orange light.
The atmosphere converts blue photons into red photons by increasing their wavelength.
The Sun emits only red light at sunrise and sunset.

explanation: Near the horizon, sunlight travels through a longer atmospheric path. Shorter visible wavelengths are scattered more strongly, reducing their contribution to direct sunlight. The remaining beam is relatively richer in red and orange wavelengths. Scattering does not convert blue photons into red photons.

title: Tyndall effect versus ordinary transmission
question: A narrow beam of white light passes through two containers. Container P contains clean water without appreciable suspended particles; container Q contains a colloid with particles that scatter the beam. An observer views each container from the side. Which observation best identifies the Tyndall effect?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="q11beam" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6Z" fill="#F59E0B" /></marker></defs><rect x="48" y="40" width="105" height="105" rx="6" fill="#93C5FD" fill-opacity=".2" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="197" y="40" width="105" height="105" rx="6" fill="#93C5FD" fill-opacity=".2" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M8 92 L335 92" stroke="#F59E0B" stroke-width="2.5" marker-end="url(#q11beam)" /><path d="M215 92 L225 69 M235 92 L247 116 M256 92 L270 70 M276 92 L290 110" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="1.8" /><g fill="#64748B"><circle cx="218" cy="72" r="2" /><circle cx="232" cy="115" r="2" /><circle cx="260" cy="67" r="2" /><circle cx="284" cy="119" r="2" /><circle cx="248" cy="105" r="2" /><circle cx="277" cy="77" r="2" /></g><text x="100" y="28" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">P: clean water</text><text x="249" y="28" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Q: colloid</text><text x="100" y="164" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Beam less visible</text><text x="249" y="164" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Beam visible sideways</text></svg>

options.text: The beam becomes visible in P solely because light travels more slowly in water.
The beam is visible in both containers only because water refracts it at the walls.
The beam is visible from the side in Q because colloidal particles scatter light towards the observer.
The particles in Q absorb every wavelength and re-emit only white light.

explanation: Colloidal particles scatter light in different directions, making the beam visible from the side. This is the Tyndall effect. Ordinary refraction at the container walls is not the explanation, and scattering is not equivalent to complete absorption followed by re-emission.

title: Electromagnetic spectrum: wavelength order
question: An electromagnetic spectrum chart places gamma rays at the short-wavelength end and radio waves at the long-wavelength end. The visible band lies between ultraviolet and infrared. Which statement correctly describes the chart?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 165" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="43" width="326" height="34" rx="3" fill="#CBD5E1" fill-opacity=".45" stroke="#64748B" /><rect x="12" y="43" width="46" height="34" fill="#7C3AED" /><rect x="58" y="43" width="46" height="34" fill="#6366F1" /><rect x="104" y="43" width="46" height="34" fill="#3B82F6" /><rect x="150" y="43" width="48" height="34" fill="#16A34A" /><rect x="198" y="43" width="46" height="34" fill="#F59E0B" /><rect x="244" y="43" width="46" height="34" fill="#EA580C" /><rect x="290" y="43" width="48" height="34" fill="#DC2626" /><g font-size="9" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle"><text x="35" y="35">Gamma</text><text x="81" y="35">X-ray</text><text x="127" y="35">UV</text><text x="174" y="35">Visible</text><text x="221" y="35">IR</text><text x="267" y="35">Micro</text><text x="314" y="35">Radio</text></g><path d="M20 103 L330 103" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M20 98 L20 108 M330 98 L330 108" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="20" y="122" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Shorter wavelength</text><text x="330" y="122" text-anchor="end" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Longer wavelength</text><text x="175" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Not to scale</text></svg>

options.text: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths and highest frequencies; radio waves have the longest wavelengths and lowest frequencies.
Gamma rays have the longest wavelengths because they carry the most energy.
Radio waves have higher frequencies than X-rays because their wavelengths are longer.
All seven regions have the same wavelength but differ only in their ability to penetrate matter.

explanation: In vacuum, c=flambda, so frequency and wavelength are inversely related. Gamma rays occupy the high-frequency, short-wavelength end; radio waves occupy the low-frequency, long-wavelength end. Photon energy E=hf is greatest for gamma rays, not because their wavelengths are long but because their frequencies are high.

title: Electromagnetic radiation: identifying the correct detector
question: An experimental arrangement shows a source of invisible radiation directed at a fluorescent screen, a photographic plate, and a thermopile. The question concerns identifying ultraviolet radiation rather than infrared radiation or X-rays. Which is the most appropriate conclusion for detecting ultraviolet radiation in a school-level experiment?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="18" y="54" width="56" height="52" rx="5" fill="#64748B" fill-opacity=".15" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="46" y="75" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">UV</text><text x="46" y="89" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">source</text><path d="M74 80 L140 80" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2.5" /><rect x="140" y="35" width="65" height="90" fill="#A7F3D0" fill-opacity=".3" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="172" y="72" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Fluorescent</text><text x="172" y="85" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">screen</text><path d="M205 80 L245 80" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2.5" /><rect x="245" y="45" width="85" height="70" rx="4" fill="#CBD5E1" fill-opacity=".3" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="287" y="72" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Observation</text><text x="287" y="85" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">point</text><text x="175" y="151" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Radiation is invisible to the unaided eye</text></svg>

options.text: A thermopile is the only possible detector because ultraviolet radiation is identical to infrared radiation.
A fluorescent material can emit visible light under ultraviolet illumination, allowing the radiation's presence to be inferred.
A radio receiver detects ultraviolet radiation because all electromagnetic waves are interchangeable in detectors.
A prism alone proves the presence of ultraviolet radiation because ultraviolet always appears as a visible violet band.

explanation: Certain fluorescent materials absorb ultraviolet radiation and emit visible light. This provides an indirect means of detection. Ultraviolet is beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum, so it cannot be identified as an ordinary visible violet band. Detectors must be appropriate to the radiation being measured.

title: Rainbow formation: dispersion and internal reflection
question: A ray of sunlight enters a spherical raindrop, refracts and disperses into colours, reflects internally once, and refracts again on leaving the drop. Red and violet emerge in different directions. Which explanation best describes the primary rainbow?

explanation:
best describes the primary rainbow?

A) It is formed by reflection alone; refraction and dispersion are unnecessary.

B) It is formed because droplets emit seven new colours when sunlight heats them.

C) It results from diffraction of sunlight around raindrops, with all wavelengths following the same path.

D) Refraction and dispersion occur at entry, internal reflection occurs, and further refraction occurs at exit; red emerges at a larger primary-rainbow angle from the antisolar direction than violet.

**Correct Answer: D**

**Reason:** The primary rainbow involves refraction and dispersion at entry, one internal reflection, and refraction on exit. Red light is deviated less overall than violet. Consequently, red appears on the outer edge of the primary rainbow, at a larger angular radius from the antisolar point than violet. Reflection alone cannot explain the colour separation.

title: Pure versus impure spectrum
question: Arrangement P uses a narrow slit and a prism to form a spectrum on a screen. Arrangement Q uses a broad slit with the same prism and screen, so the images of the slit for different wavelengths overlap. Which modification most directly improves the purity of the spectrum?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 350 205" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="80" y="20" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">P: narrow slit</text><text x="265" y="20" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Q: broad slit</text><rect x="20" y="35" width="12" height="65" fill="#64748B" fill-opacity=".4" stroke="#64748B" /><rect x="203" y="35" width="22" height="65" fill="#64748B" fill-opacity=".4" stroke="#64748B" /><polygon points="60,42 60,95 100,68" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".2" stroke="#2563EB" /><polygon points="244,42 244,95 284,68" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity=".2" stroke="#2563EB" /><path d="M32 67 L60 67 M100 68 L155 43 M100 68 L155 53 M100 68 L155 63 M100 68 L155 73 M100 68 L155 83 M100 68 L155 93" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M225 67 L244 67 M284 68 L325 43 M284 68 L325 53 M284 68 L325 63 M284 68 L325 73 M284 68 L325 83 M284 68 L325 93" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="155" y="35" width="4" height="65" fill="#64748B" /><rect x="325" y="35" width="4" height="65" fill="#64748B" /><text x="157" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Screen</text><text x="327" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Screen</text><text x="80" y="151" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Sharper colour bands</text><text x="265" y="151" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Greater overlap</text><text x="175" y="186" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Schematic optical arrangements</text></svg>

options.text: Widen the slit further so that more light of every wavelength reaches the screen.
Replace the prism with a plane-parallel glass slab, which separates all wavelengths more strongly.
Use a narrow slit and suitable optics to reduce overlap between the images corresponding to different wavelengths.
Increase the screen brightness until overlapping wavelengths become distinguishable without changing the optical arrangement.

explanation: A narrow slit reduces the width of each spectral image, reducing overlap between neighbouring colours. A broad slit tends to produce an impure spectrum because images of different wavelengths overlap. Brightness alone does not improve spectral separation.
